REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: For a copy of the report made by the advisory committee under the chairmanship of Mr. J. Coon, set up by order in council P.C. 2-584, and of all correspondence, recommendations and other documents in the possession of the government in relation thereto.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the report in question is really an intradepartmental communication. It was asked for the other day by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwel'l), and I stated then, as I now state, that I regard it as confidential and not properly producible. If the hon. member wishes to redraft the motion so as to request the production of letters to and from the department respecting the matters dealt with in the report, I will have no objection. But the report itself I regard as confidential.

maintopic: REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
On the
point as to the confidential nature of the report, my understanding is that this report is the result of a public order in council which either was or could be tabled, and that there is nothing in the order in council to indicate that the report when made would be confidential. I regard this as a public document, and the house is entitled to have i:t. I am sure it would be a matter of keen interest to the public, especially to people in Ottawa. The Minister, knowing what is in it, declares it to be confidential; but that was not the basis of the order in council.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I do not know how many times I am entitled to speak on the motion. I have made my position clear. There are many orders in council setting up departmental committees and interdepartmental committees which prepare reports containing advice for ministers. Certainly these have never been regarded as producible in the House Of Commons. The government must take the responsibility for what they do after they get such advice as they are able to secure, but in my judgment the advice they get is not a public document.

maintopic: REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
This is not a report
of a departmental committee. I would point out to the house that the chairman of this committee was not connected with any department, nor was he a government employee; he was a person entirely outside the public service. Therefore I do not understand in what respect the committee can be regarded as a departmental committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
He was just as much an
officer of the department when he was sitting with the other members of that committee as are many hundreds of persons who are brought in temporarily to assist the government from time to time and who are now and have been during the war years connected with the government service.

maintopic: REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
How much was Mr. Coon paid?
Motions for Papers

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE ADVISORY COMMITTEE

maintopic: REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I asked
a question about this matter the other day, and I am glad it has been brought up again particularly in this form. The Coon report deals with conditions within the civil service of Canada. If a report has been made to any department-particularly, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Ottawa West, when it has been made by a man not a member of one of our departments, a man who comes from outside the service and outside the city of Ottawa-this house should know what conditions have been revealed and what suggestions have been made with regard to the remedying of any conditions that may be bad. To my mind this is not a report which concerns the treasury board only or the government only; it is a report which concerns the House of Commons. The house should insist that the report be tabled in order that we may be apprised of conditions within the civil service, which, is the civil service, not of the government, not of the ministers, not of the treasury board, but of the parliament of Canada of which this chamber is a part. I hope that the house will insist on the tabling of this document.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
If I may speak again, the
same observations would apply to the report of every advisory committee, without exception. Every year the advisory committee to the wheat board presents a report, but we do not produce it, and there are scores of other advisory committees.

maintopic: REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
They
should.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That is the issue, and I
am stating my position. If the government sets up advisory committees to advise ministers or to advise the government, where the government is of the opinion that such advice is confidential, then the reports must be regarded as confidential. I do not regard this as being in any other category.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I for one am unconvinced by the minister's argument against the tabling of this report. The press of Canada and the public generally have looked upon this committee as a committee which would make a report of much consequence, of much value and of much importance to the government. Its deliberations were not confidential so far as the press were concerned, because time after time they were referred to. The position ought to be made clear so far as the House of Commons is concerned. The minister has mentioned the advisory committee of
[Mr. Homuth.3
the wheat board. This is also a matter of policy, and I think that question should be deliberated upon by this house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: And twenty others.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: There should be a decision on these matters. I propose to vote in favour of the tabling of this report as called for by the hon. member for Ottawa West. I consider that this is a matter which should be pressed to the limit and we are prepared to do that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: The issue is there and perhaps it should be settled; I do not know. If we are going to set up advisory committees, a great many of them by orders in council, if we are going to set up interdepartmental committees, departmental committees and so forth, every reason for the making public of this report will apply to the reports of those committees. If that is what the government must do in the future, let us have it settled.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: The minister is confusing the issue. This is not an interdepartmental committee. When the minister asks civil servants under him to set up an interdepartmental committee, with a deputy minister or someone else as chairman, the chairman of that committee is in an entirely different position from that of an outsider like Mr. Coon, who was brought in for a definite purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Not a bit.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
maintopic: REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I would call the attention of the house to the fact that we are not in committee.

maintopic: REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel that this report should be tabled. This is not a question of government policy, where secrecy should be maintained, where the contents of a report should not be divulged. The civil servants of Canada are affected in connection with their relations as employees of the government of Canada. A request has been made for the tabling of this report concerning civil servants and their employment. Surely the civil servants have the right to know what attention has been given to their representations. Surely they have the right to expect that members of the House of Commons will be acquainted with their conditions and with the result of any investigation that has been held. That should not affect government policy, and there should be no question of government responsibility in keeping secret the contents of this report dealing with the welfare of the civil servants. The members of this House of Commons are definitely inter-

speechtext:
I wish to ask the Minister of Labour a question. Press dispatches indicate that Doctor Walter J. Couper, who has been executive assistant to the minister and the deputy minister of labour, and who is reported to have expressed in public dissatisfaction with the man-power policy of the department-a matter which was dealt with, I believe, by some hon. member during the debate-has severed his connections with the department

and is returning to his former position with the International labour office. Will the Minister of Labour kindly inform the house as to whether or not Doctor Couper severed his connections at the instance of the minister or the deputy minister of labour?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: MAN-POWER POSITION OP DOCTOR W. J. COUPER-REPORT IN TORONTO "GLOBE AND MAIL"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I read in last Saturday's Globe and, Mail the news item referred to by the leader of the opposition. I was much surprised that two unfair and unjust implications had been included. One of them was:
It is regarded as significant however that Doctor Couper was the last of some sixteen advisers, all in a more or less technical capacity, who have parted company with the department since Elliott M. Little resigned as director of national selective service.
The other is:
Possibility that Doctor Couper's views on the administration of selective service, and the general situation as to man-power, are at variance with the labour minister is not being overlooked, especially since, no later than the second week in April, he forcefully and clearly expressed his opinions in an address in Toronto on the cause of the labour situation.
I do not think I can give a better answer to the leader of the opposition than to read the text of a telegram dispatched by Doctor Couper on Saturday last after he read the news item about himself in the Globe and Mail. It is as follows.
Ottawa, June 5, 1943.
Editor
Globe and Mail Toronto, Ontario.
It is true that the possibility of my return to duty on the staff of the International Labour Office is currently under discussion. It is not true as implied in Cragg's story that I have broken with the Minister of Labour on the question of man-power policy. I was and am a friend of Elliott Little but that does not affect my views about government policy. If you will obtain from Morley, manager, Industrial Accident Prevention Associations, steno-typist transcript my address from which you purport to quote, you will see that by wrenching statements from their context you create an impression exactly opposite to that which I intended to convey and which I think the full text does convey.
W. J. Couper.
I looked for this telegram in this morning's Globe and Mail, but I did not find it there. I think in fairness to myself-and to Doctor Couper more than myself, because he is not in the house to speak for himself, and in the nature of things cannot be-this newspaper might at least have had the decency to print a retraction of the story of last Saturday.

speechtext:
I have a question to direct to the government or to the minister responsible for seeing that the censorship rules are carried out. It is based on two newspaper articles, and I trust the house will bear with me for a moment while I explain the basis on which my question is put.
A newspaper article appeared in the Toronto Evening Telegram of May 31, and it is entitled:
Missing Son's Voice on Air from Berlin.
Chases Worries of Parents in Toronto.
The article refers to a broadcast on the previous Friday by Doctor Goebbels, who stated that on the following day a certain young man from Toronto who is a prisoner of war in Germany would broadcast. The newspaper has pictures of the father and mother and members of the boy's family. It gives a full account of the feelings of the parents as they heard their son's voice. The newspaper states that "it brought unbounded joy to his parents", and goes on to say:
As tears of happiness rolled down their cheeks, Mr. and Mrs. Morrison instantly recognized their son's voice.
I bring this to the attention of the government because Doctor Goebbels is endeavouring to have people in Canada listen to his broadcasts and this is one way of attracting their attention. The Canadian people, by listening to these broadcasts, will listen to many others; and as the News of June 5 states, the paper is helping the doctor. I am not suggesting that it is doing so knowingly. I know that the Toronto Telegram would not do anything to assist the enemy ; it is one of the most patriotic papers in this dominion; but I do feel that unwittingly, by giving such publicity, by informing people that their sons' voices are likely to be heard over the German radio, it may cause many people to listen to German propaganda. Someone says, what if they do? Well, that is the way the Germans have carried on this war. They are spreading propaganda by such methods as this, and I feel it should not be encouraged. This particular boy had been missing for many months. He had not been reported by the Red Cross. The Red Cross society is doing a splendid service to Canada by reporting, as soon as it possibly can, all men who are missing. If the people of Canada are to get news of missing airmen and sailors-[DOT]

speakeroldname: Hon. CYRUS MACMILLAN (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
The minister has instructed me to answer a few questions that were asked

War Appropriation-Air Services
in the last two or three days. The first question was from the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon).

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: A good place to start.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
A splendid place. The question was with, reference to chaplains. The answer is:
1.	(a) Chaplains are not granted any powers of command and therefore only honorary rank is provided for them.
(b)	Chaplains are not subject to accept or assume the full responsibilities of the rank granted them in comparison with all other R.C.A.F. officers; that is, they are not detailed to assume all the ordinary duties normally allotted to an officer, such as drill parades, orderly officer, etc., etc.
(c)	The practice of granting honorary rank to chaplains follows the custom adopted by the other armed forces of Canada and the armed forces of the United Kingdom.
2.	Although appointed to honorary rank, R.C.A.F. chaplains are paid at the same rates as other special reserve, non-flying list officers of equal rank.
The next question was from the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling):
Is all signal equipment used by the R.C.A.F. in Canada of Canadian make?
The answer is, no. Approximately 50 per cent is Canadian; 15 per cent, American, and 35 per cent, United Kingdom.
Do Canadian capital companies come into competition with regular commercial signal equipment companies?
The answer is, yes. Research Enterprises Limited handle all secret radio equipment and were set up for this purpose.
The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) asked in regard to the situation in Canada with respect to transfers from the army to the air force for training as aircrew. Direct transfers are not possible under existing regulations. Personnel of the army desiring to serve in the RiCA.F. must be discharged by the army before enlistment in the R.C.A.F. Regulations governing discharges from the army for the purpose of enlisting in any other force are set out in Canadian army routine order No. 1030 dated May 7, 1941.
Only applications from candidates for enlistment as aircrew and such other highly specialized trades as may be urgently required are considered from personnel in the army. A soldier of an active unit of the Canadian army desiring entry into another service must first submit an application in writing to his
commanding officer requesting discharge for the purpose of enlisting into the service concerned. If the application is concurred in, the commanding officer will then forward his recommendation, accompanied by the soldier's application, to the nearest recruiting centre of the service concerned. If it is decided to accept the soldier for service in the R.C.A.F. the air force recruiting officer will notify the soldier's commanding officer by letter stating the trade in which he will be enlisted and the date he is to report for duty. Army discharge proceedings are then commenced.
At the present time, negotiations between the army and the air force are proceeding with the object of increasing the flow of men desiring aircrew training from the army and also to arrange for enlistment into the army of men who have failed in their aircrew training in the R.C.A.F. Final arrangements have not been made.
The hon. member for Fort William asked with regard to the Memorial Cross: Who gets the Silver Cross; how can distant relations get it; what are the regulations? As hon. members doubtless know, the Silver Cross is a memorial to airmen who were killed in action or who died while on active service or from causes attributable to service in the air force, either while serving on active duty or subsequent to discharge from the said force. The Silver Cross is granted to mothers and/or widows of Canadian airmen who have died in the service of their country during the present war. In case, after becoming entitled to the cross, the widow or mother has died, the cross will be delivered to the eldest of the airman's next of kin.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The eldest female next of kin?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
No, the eldest next of kin. Air force administrative order A.64/2 sets out the regulations, and is as follows:
Regulations pertaining to the grant of the Memorial Cross to the mothers and/or widows of Canadian airmen who have died in the service of their country during the present war. Reason of Issue
1.	A Memorial Cross will be issued as a memento of persona] loss and sacrifice on the part of mothers and widows of Canadian airmen, who have laid down their lives for their country during the present war.
Description of Cross
2.	The cross will be a cross patonce in silver, suspended by a purple ribbon; and at the end of the upright a crown; at the foot, and at the end of either arm, a maple leaf; in the centre,

War Appropriation-Air Services
within a wreath of laurel, with royal cipher "G.R.I." It will be engraved with the number and/or name of the airman commemorated.
3.	A cross will be issued to the widow or mother in respect of every airman who was survived by either. If both survive him, two crosses will be issued, one to each.
4.	If, after becoming entitled to the cross, the widow or mother has died or dies, the cross will be delivered to the eldest of the airman's next of kin.
In Respect of Whom Issued
5.	The cross will be issued in respect of each airman, who:
(a)	was killed in action; or
(b)	died, whilst on active service; or
(c)	died or dies from causes attributable to service in the air forces whether while serving on active service or subsequent to his discharge from the said forces;
Provided that where death occurs subsequent to discharge, the Memorial Cross will be issued to the widow only if she was married to the airman at the time of his discharge.
Proof Required
6.	Every applicant for the issue ,of a cross must produce such proof of death, service and eligibility as may be required by the Minister of National Defence for Air in respect of Canadian airmen.
Authority
7.	The decision of the Minister of National Defence for Air shall be final in all matters pertaining to the issue of the cross in respect of Canadian airmen.
8.	In the foregoing paragraphs;-
_ (a) "Widow" includes the legal widow of the airman killed and the unmarried widow who is pensionable by^ reason of the airman's death, but does not include a widow as so defined who,-
(i)	Is known to be of dissolute character.
(ii)	Was at the time of the airman's death, separated from him by agreement or legal process.
(b)	"Mother" means the woman who gave birth to the airman.
(c)	"Airman" means any person, male or female, who served in the Royal Canadian Air Force or who having been ordinarily resident in Canada on the 10th of September, 1939, or at any time during a period of 10 years prior to this date, served in the air forces of his majesty or any of his allies.
9.	These regulations shall have force and effect as of and from the 1st September, 1939, and are made and established by order in council P C. 4210, dated 27th August, 1940, as amended by order in council P.C. 2135, dated 28th March, 1941.
On Friday afternoon the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black) asked a question with reference to the delivery of cables overseas. Postal letter telegrams are sent from cablehead, where they are received in England, by mail to the base post office where the last posting of the personnel is determined; the cable is then forwarded again by mail to the

unit concerned. All direct cables are telegraphed from cablehead to the base post office at Manchester; then when the posting is determined they are forwarded by mail to the unit concerned. In all cases when telegrams or cables are received at the addressee's unit, they are delivered to him as quickly as possible. On account of the amount of mail handled at the base post office inevitably there are some delays, but there may be some at the units also, especially when the addressees are absent on operational duties.

The hon. member for York West asked whether we will use cracked gasoline in aircraft. The answer is, yes. Tests have been carried on at No. 2 S.F.T.S. for the last six months, and the MeColl-Frontenac product has been approved for 80 and 87 octane gasoline. Tests are still being carried out for other companies. The hon. member also asked a question with respect to the R.C.A.F. staff college, and if there is any suggestion of adding an R.C.A.F. college after the war. The answer is that a provisional syllabus for the course of training at the R.C.A.F. staff college has been drawn up and a suitable location for the school has been decided upon. The objective of the R.C.A.F. staff college is to give selected R.C.A.F. officers of relatively senior rank instruction in advanced administrative and staff work applicable to present day service conditions. There is no intention at the present time to add an R.C.A.F. college after the war, but the question may be considered at the appropriate time.
Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury); When would that be, if not after the war?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
The staff college is at Fiavelle House, and it will be open about July 15. The hon. member for York West also asked whether an attempt is being made to get ground crew wherever possible from those unfit for aircrew and, if so, what categories we were taking. The answer is that

War Appropriation-Air Services
an attempt is being made wherever possible to fill ground crew quota with men physically unfit for aircrew duties. The medical category for ground crew has been lowered from A4B to A4HBH.
The hon. member for York West asked a question with respect to sea rescue. I shall try to summarize the answer, which is relatively long.
What was the question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: Have any measures been developed for air-sea rescues. Early in the war steps were taken to establish an air-sea rescue service by the commissioning of vessels on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, oceangoing vessels in addition to the salvage vessels and crash boats. Details of this cannot well be given. The hon. member may have them privately. Rather remarkable developments have taken place in respect of the type of emergency equipment provided. Hon. members are no doubt familiar with the report of that airman of matchless courage, Captain Rickenbacker, following his miraculous rescue after twenty-one days on a rubber raft. No doubt hon. members are familiar with the recommendations he made some months ago. The information is that practically all these recommendations have been carried into effect, with the result that the risk has been greatly decreased. That includes, of course, the provision of collapsible rubber boats which are automatically inflated, and the providing to each member of the crew of every Royal Canadian Air Force aircraft operating over the ocean of a Mae West life jacket, and also heavy clothing, with a special emergency supply apparatus containing food, water and other equipment. Then, there is a continuous watch throughout the twenty-four hours on the two coasts. There is further secret information which the hon. member may read.
Has Canada tried the carrying of small motor launches by aeroplanes, so that they can be deposited where crews are to be rescued?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: Not up to the present time.

I
notice they have them in Great Britain.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
Development along
that line is proceeding, however.
The hon. member for York West asked a question with respect to the commissioning or promotion of prisoners of war. Negotiations with Germany have been undertaken through
the Department of External Affairs. Although there can be no definite statement regarding what the decision has been, there is no reason at the present time to doubt that the suggestion will be carried forward. Negotiations are pending with Italy, and it is not considered advisable by the department to discuss them in public at the present time, because such discussions might jeopardize their success.
The hon. member for York West asked respecting categories of aircrew, and concerning percentage of training received in Canada. The details are these:
Of bombing navigators, 94 per cent of the output receive all their training in Canada, and 6 per cent in the United Kingdom. Those who complete their training in the United Kingdom do 77 per cent of their training in Canada and 23 per cent in the United Kingdom.
Of general navigators, none complete their training in Canada, all completing their training in the United Kingdom. In this group 74 per cent of the training is done in Canada, and 26 per cent in the United Kingdom.
Of wireless navigators, 19 per cent of the output complete their training in Canada, and 81 per cent in the United Kingdom. Those who complete their training in the United Kingdom do 81 per cent of their training in Canada, and 19 per cent in the United Kingdom.
Of air bombers, none complete their training in Canada, all being completed in the United Kingdom. Seventy-three per cent of their training is in Canada, and 27 per cent in the United Kingdom.
Of' wireless air gunners, 86 per cent of production complete their training in Canada, and 14 per cent in the United Kingdom. Those who complete their training in the United Kingdom do 76 per cent of their training in Canada, and 24 per cent in the United Kingdom.
In respect of air gunners, those who complete their training in the United Kingdom do 58 per cent in Canada, and 42 per cent in the United Kingdom.
In respect of pilots, those who complete their training in the United Kingdom do 76 per cent of their courses in Canada and 24 per cent in the United Kingdom.
That includes fighter and bomber pilots?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
Yes. The hon. member for York West asked a question with respect to experience in connection with shearling in wool. On the basis of many months of

War Appropriation-Air Services
fundamental research, developmental work and field trials, the use of shearling in flying suits has been shown to be less satisfactory than the new type Royal Canadian Air Force flying suits for the following reasons: Greater bulkiness of shearling suit; greater weight of shearling suit; poor snag resistance of shearling leather; poorer resistance to compression loads of shearling, and therefore less thermal insulation and decreased warmth; greater retention of gas fumes in exposed shearling, including collars and the like, with increased possibility of burns following gasoline fires; shearling much less flexible than new-type suit and, last, greater cost of shearling flying suits.
The new-type "E" flying suit was developed on the basis of a questionnaire answered by over 4,100 aircrew. The detachable lining is a newly developed flexible double-pile twenty-two-ounce wool lining employing 50 per cent 64's, 20 per cent 60's, 20 per cent 56's and 10 per cent 50's, Canadian wool, with a thickness of one-half inch uncompressed.*
Shearling is still used in Royal Canadian Air Force flying boots, and due to the large stock on hand no change is contemplated in the near future.
The hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) asked with regard to payment of personnel in the United States and Alaska. Royal Canadian Air Force personnel in the United States receive their pay and allowances in United States funds, their net entitlement in Canadian dollars plus credit for loss on exchange as provided by an order in council, being converted to the equivalent in United States dollars. They are paid dollar for dollar in United States funds.
That is, they receive in United States money $1.30 a day.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
Yes, in United States money. The second question asked by the hon. member for Peterborough West was with respect to the reason for the increase in rentals. The increase is not for rentals alone. The item under consideration was for rentals, water, light, power, heating, sanitary services, renewals, repairs and other maintenance costs of properties.
The expenditures for 1942A3 in the British commonwealth air training plan included the Royal Air Force schools from July 1, 1942, to March 31, 1943, a period of nine months, whereas for 1943-44 provision must be made for a full twelve-month period for these schools. All the expansion of the British commonwealth air training programme begun in the fall of 1942 will have its full effect in

1943-44. This applies also to a very substantial expansion in construction connected with the western hemisphere operations. The greater the amount of the property to be taken care of, the higher the expenditure will be for maintenance.
Another question asked by the hon. member for Peterborough West was with regard to the special treatment given night fliers to develop their eyes. The reply is that the night vision of aircrew is tested on a special apparatus for this purpose, but details can not be given, other than privately.
Another question had reference to the use of sulpha drugs. Sulpha drugs are used in the Royal Canadian Air Force in treatment of certain infections where elaborate clinical investigation has proved their worth. A greatly lessened mortality rate' from pneumonia, streptococcal infections, war wounds and the like can be attributed to the use of sulpha drugs. Their application in preventing surgical infection is recognized. There are five varieties of sulpha drugs issued for emergency use to prevent infection in injuries and wounds, until the patient can be given more special medical attention.
The men have this themselves, have they?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: Yes. The hon. member asked a question respecting a death resulting from inoculation at No. 35 elementary flying training school. This matter has been studied in the greatest detail. The results of the special investigation have been prepared for the coroner's inquest. No informed report can be given until the findings of the inquest are received. That report is expected within the next few days, and the hon. member will be given a copy.

Is that the case at
Neepawa?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes, from inoculations.
The hon. member mentioned the coroner's inquest. Is he not following out in Manitoba the plan adopted in Ontario, under which there is no coroner's inquest?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
This happens to be a
special case. As a result of inoculations fif.ty-two or fifty-three people were made ill and the thing became a little complicated because of having to decide whether the toxoid itself was defective or whether it was faulty inoculation. The Connaught laboratories prepare nearly all the fluids or whatever it is that are used in inoculations, and they sent a Mr. Fraser out there.

War Appropriation-Air Services
No relation.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The department of health of Manitoba has a Doctor Jackson there. Inquiries have been made but we have not had a full report. Everything that can be done to find out who should be blamed will be done. The coroner's inquest will follow our inquiry. This will be under the presidency of Doctor Jackson of Manitoba.
Mr. MeCANN: Is this a special investigation of just one case?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It is a special investigation. As a rule we do not have a public inquiry or investigation, as my hon. friend knows, but this was a case where the death should be inquired into.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) asked a question with respect to the supply of water at Mossbank, and the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) asked a similar question about Assiniboia and Dafoe. These questions will have to be answered by the Department of Transport, as that department is responsible for the supplying of water to building sites. This information has been requested and will be given later. The hon. member for Davenport asked about the type of runway at the airfield at the Pas, but this information is secret. However, I shall send it to the hon. member privately.
The hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy), the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Ross), the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Hoblitzell) and the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) inquired about provisions being made with regard to inteiTupted education. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar also asked about the educational qualifications of our airmen. A total of 68,000 occupational histories of members of the air force have been checked and checking is still in progress. The information obtained is extremely impressive. First there is the fact of their youth. I think the late Mr. Binyon's line applies to these young men more emphatically than to any other group- "They went with songs to the battle, they were young". Seventy per cent of the 68,000 checked are under twenty-seven years of age, and more than half of them are between the ages of eighteen and twenty-three years. Their high standard of education is amazing, and the minister has asked me to put the following figures before you because of their impressiveness.
Of this total number of 68,000, 6,800 in round figures have university degrees or were
undergraduates at the time of enlistment; 5,500 had completed their senior matriculation, the equivalent of the first year in university; 5,600 had partly completed their senior matriculation; over 13,000 had completed their junior matriculation and 21,500 . had completed it in part-that is, one or two or three subjects yet to be passed; 1,300 had completed technical school requirements and 4,200 had partly completed technical school courses; 700 had completed teachers' courses. About 54,000 out of 68,000 had junior matriculation in part or higher qualifications.
I am sure that every hon. member looks forward to the return of these young men and the question of their rehabilitation and repatriation will be a very serious problem.

Their
interrupted education.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: I understand that the phrase "interrupted education" applies to members of the forces who were in educational institutions at the time of enlistment pursuing a course of studies or who had temporarily suspended their studies because of financial or health or other reasons. Unquestionably most of these men will wish to return and provision has been made already toward that end. Order in council P.C. 7633, passed on October 1, 1941, and amended on April 20, 1943, makes provision for their educational needs by providing for grants. This comes under the jurisdiction of the Department of Pensions and National Health, but I am sure the minister of that department will1 not mind my saying a word or two about it. The order in council provides for a grant of $10.20 per week in the case of an unmarried student and $14.40 per week in the case of a married student, with fees if required.
In addition?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: Yes. The universities are making provision to give refresher courses to these young men and women when they return. No man can say what intellectual power has been or will be lost, but we must do everything possible to help those who come back to attain their objectives. In olden days a pessimist said: Who shall restore the years that the locusts have eaten? These young people will be able to restore part of the lost years themselves if they are given assistance and encouragement and wise guidance. I am sure that nothing is closer to the heart of the minister than that.

We have been given some splendid information just now, but there is one point to which consideration should be



War Appropriation-Air Services
given, and that is the period of time that many of these men are kept in the army before being discharged. Many of these men left medical, dental and other practices, to which they are ready to go back. They will be anxious to get right back to work and will not want to be held in the army for one or two years after the war is over before being discharged.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: The suggestion is that they be given the preference.
I should think so.
Those who have positions to go to immediately.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: I understand that the universities will give them precedence in admission.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The rehabilitation system that we are working on would permit a boy with a B.A. who wanted to go on to law to go to the university to study for that profession. It would be paid for by the government of Canada to give him a chance to complete his education.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
The clause reads:
In case any discharged person becomes regularly admitted to a university and commences any such course-
I just wanted to make sure that the minister has my point. There are a great many men in the air force who were formerly practising his profession.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I think that is another problem. I do not know how we can rehabilitate the man who was practising, say, law or medicine, but as my colleague has said, there are so many who have interrupted their education to join the air force that we are trying to furnish them with an opportunity to complete it. I do not see how we could rehabilitate a man in his practice if he was a lawyer or a doctor.
Their practices are there awaiting them.
Are the benefits that are being provided for the men being provided also for the women, at the same rate?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: The answer is yes to both questions.
The women will get the same rate of benefit pay?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: The subsidy or assistance granted is the same to male and female *-but not to a married woman. That is set out in the order in council.

I think the point of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle is well taken. Many members have expressed themselves to the effect that when the war is over the men in tie armed forces should not be suddenly discharged and thrown on the labour market. I think most hon. members will agree with that as a general submission. But as the hon. member for Qu'Appelle has said, there are many men who have left the professions in which they were established. I quite agree that these men should be encouraged when the war is over to go back to their professions, if they so desire, and not be held in the forces. Then there are students, as the parliamentary assistant to the minister has stated, whose studies were interrupted. There should be no delay in allowing these men to go back to their studies so that they may qualify themselves for whatever profession they have chosen. These two classes should not be any great problem. But there is a third class, men who have no trade, no profession and no business to which to return. I trust that when the war is over this class, which is composed of the great mass of men in the armed forces, will not be suddenly thrown on the labour market with nothing to do.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman) asked two or three questions: He asked: "Is there to be a fleet air arm formed in Canada?" The question of forming a fleet air arm in Canada has been under discussion but no definite decision has been arrived at. He also asked: "What becomes of obsolete material?" Obsolete material is disposed of as follows:
(1)	Retained in the service for instructional use.
(2)	Sold to civil air lines in mining communities or to contractors et cetera, who may require this equipment.
(3)	Or issued to war extension training programme schools and air cadet squadrons for instructional purposes.
(4)	If the equipment is not required for any of these purposes it is reduced to produce and disposed of by sale as scrap.
The hon. member for Rosedale also asked:
Is all equipment in depots modern?
Yes; stocks at equipment depots are reviewed continuously to ensure that equipment declared obsolete does not accumulate. Particulars of the obsolete items held are submitted to air force headquarters for disposal instructions.
The hon. member also asked for a comparison of personnel strength. At No. 2 Service Flying Training School at Uplands comparison of personnel strength as at May 31, 1941, and May 31, 1943, shows the following:

It will be seen that while the number of aircrew in training showed an increase of thirty-four per cent, the increase in staff was only sixteen per cent. Thus the ratio of staff to pupils decreased from 5-06 to one to the present figure of 4-38 to one.
The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) asked how decorations were awarded. Recommendations for honours and awards may be submitted under the following classifications:
(a)	Gallantry awards for any specific act of gallantry or series of acts of bravery. These may be submitted as immediate at any time or included in the periodic lists.
(b)	(i) Chivalry awards for extreme meritorious service and devotion to duty. These may only be considered in the periodic lists.
(ii) Certain gallantry awards may also be awarded for devotion to duty and meritorious service, i.e., A.F.C., A.F.M., B.E.M., "M.I.D." and commendations.
I have a list here of the honours and awards granted to air force personnel, excluding those of last week. Hon. members might be interested in knowing that the total of awards for gallantry is 479.
The hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Cardiff) asked a question with reference to security guards:
Have they been given a chance to remuster to a trade of their choice or will they be transferred to another trade arbitrarily without any choice in the matter?
Yes. Given the necessary qualifications and provided there is room within the establishment of the trade preferred, security guards are given ample opportunity to remuster to the trade of their preference. For example, in the recent amalgamation of service police and security duties, all security guards were individually interviewed to ascertain how many wished to remuster to the trade of service police; several hundred were so remustered by their own expressed choice, but none was remustered against his will. Those who were not remustered to service police appeared before duly constituted trade selection boards to be remustered to other trades, according to their several capabilities and expressed preferences.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The hon. member for Cam-rose (Mr. Marshall) asked a question with regard to radio mechanics. It is a long story but I will try to make it as brief as possible.
TFar Appropriation-Air Services
In January, 1941, we received a request from Sir Gerald Campbell to see if we could not recruit in Canada radio mechanics for the Royal Air Force. I happen to have discussed this matter of radio mechanics with a higher authority, Mr. Churchill, in England, and he ascribes the victory in the battle of Britain largely to radio mechanics or radio locators, and the United Kingdom government allotted the highest priority to them. The original request came in October, 1940, from Sir Gerald Campbell, then high commissioner. It had nothing to do with the joint empire training agreement; it was, so to speak, an extra. At that time they asked for 1,000 radio mechanics, but as things went on, eventually the request came for 5,000. They required a very high standard; so much so, that we thought the best people we could get would be university students. As a matter of fact in May, 1941, I made a speech calling on students of the universities to undertake this radio mechanic training, and we sent these people to the different universities all across Canada to follow a university course. Somehow or other we seem to have demanded too high qualifications. We had lawyers, doctors, clergymen: for instance, there is a clergyman up in the Hebrides who is a private in the air force, and a headmaster of a Toronto school who is somewhere in the Faroe islands, holding the position of acting lance corporal without pay. Evidently we rather exaggerated the required qualifications, but the man who invented the apparatus thought, like most other inventors, that he needed the best possible - men to handle it, and he sold us the idea of obtaining the best educated men we could. We were asked for 5,000 and we supplied 5,000. These unfortunate fellows have been sent all over the world. Some of them went to West Africa, some to Singapore, some elsewhere. Nearly all are of the class of university student, and of course, they did not get the advancement which one would expect people of that class to get; they are still LAC's. This is nobody's fault, or if it is anybody's fault I suppose it is ours, because the work seemed so important. I must say I am more responsible than anybody else. I said, "We will send the best we can get," because apparently this was the most important thing that could be done. In any case they went overseas and, as I say, did not get much in the way of promotion.
But wTe have now provided for radio mechanics of two kinds. I cannot explain the details, because they are very secret. There are six categories. There is radio mechanic, air:	he is the man who looks after whatever
radio machines they put in the aeroplanes.

War Appropriation-Air Services
There is also radio mechanic, ground, who gets the radio locations from different parts and has all these secret devices. Apparently the ground men are all right. They have been sent all over the world: some are in Kenya, some in West Africa, others at Cape Town, and everywhere they are getting on pretty well. The trouble with the radio mechanics has been that this radio business changes so quickly that before they are fully trained their machines are obsolescent, so that they have had to begin all over again and learn a new system. The result is that they could not get promotion. They would be trade-tested on machine A, and 'by the time they got to their assigned place machine B was installed, and they were out of luck.

The course was about
six months, was it not?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I believe the university-trained boys had two months in Canada plus whatever they had in England. For a while they were unemployed or misemployed; there is no question about that. But now the thing has straightened itself out. I believe that, of the 5,000 required, all but 200 have been sent over; 638 have received their commissions, and now every one of them gets trade pay; he is either a corporal or a sergeant; and they are trade-tested by Canadian boards. So that the situation is pretty well cleared up. For a while it was very interesting. I do not know that I can say much more, except that the boys are happier than they were a year ago. We sent highly educated people-for instance, lawyers-to do what a man should do with a hammer and chisel: that is about the size of it. It was our fault, I think, somebody told us to require too much.
Can they get still further promotion? Is there anything else for them to go up to?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That has to do with the commissioning policy. I do not know of any class we have sent over who are more under the Royal Air Force. They are mixed up everywhere; they are not in Canadian squadrons. I do not know who is in charge of them. There is a group of some kind, and they can get commissions; they are on the basis of ten per cent on graduation and ten per cent for service in the field. After all it is not so bad, for what are they, really? They are signallers.
I was going to ask the minister how they compare with the army, who did more or less the same thing but did it through the signal corps.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The complaint that my hon. friend has is that the army men get promotions more quickly. I am not sure about that, because I do not think the army enlisted very many of them. They may have enlisted them as straight signallers.
Are they R.A.F or R.C.A.F.?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: They are R.C.A.F. They wear R.C.A.F. uniforms, but their careers are dictated by R.A.F. If they go to England they can be sent to the Shetlands or anywhere else.
I believe the army did the same thing, and the course was six months.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not think so. There are signallers who know the radio mechanic's job, but I do not think they went out to get them as radio mechanics.

I think the Minister of National Defence for Air showed his good sense in placing extra work upon his parliamentary assistant, for he does it well; which proves the old proverb that two heads are better than one, especially when they are good. It also proves that the appointment of parliamentary assistants is of splendid value to this house. On behalf of those in the homes where the boys have lost their mothers and the next of kin of casualties will receive the Silver Cross, I would thank the minister and his parliamentary assistant for this consideration. It will be like a drop of sweet oil poured into a very tender wound; because when a boy loses his mother when he is young, and an aunt or an older sister or someone else comes in and takes the place of that mother, she appreciates very much this Silver Cross, which tells her and all Canada that the ministers in charge have a little bit of heart and sympathy. I thank them.
Has the parliamentary assistant supplied all the answers which he has thus far obtained?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: No; I have some more to give.	.
Why not finish them? I am interested in an answer to the question about civil servants in the air force.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
The hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) asked a question, which I will answer now. He asked, is there a new field in Wainwright, Alberta? The answer is yes, a single landing strip 5,000

War Appropriation-Air Services
feet long and 200 feet wide, near Wainwright. It is built to carry air exercises in connection with airmen's training.
Will the parliamentary assistant state where that field is situated? Has it anything to do with the army training school which is now located very close to Wainwright?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: The only information I have is that it is at Wainwright, Alberta.

I know, but a large training centre is being built there at the present time for the army. It is the old Wainwright buffalo park, a huge place, and quite a large amount of building is going on. Has the parliamentary assistant any information as to the exact location of this airport?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
I will try to give that information this evening. The member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) asked a question with regard to the expenditure last year and this jmar classified according to the three branches of the department, oversea^, commonwealth air training and western command. The estimated expenditures for 1942-43 are: C.A.T.P. $45,000.000; western hemisphere operation, $65,000,000, or a total of $110,000,000; for 1943-44 the B.C.A.T.P. is $35,022,282 and western hemisphere operations, S5S,398,818, or a total, as contained in the sheet before you, of $93,421,100. It will be noted that there are no expenditures overseas for 1942-43 and no provision is included in the estimate for such expenditures for 1943-44.
The member for Weyburn asked another question: what has been done to localize training, to eliminate the excessive use of railway travel.
Personnel are posted in such a manner as to minimize the use of transportation. In the case of staff personnel, movements must, of necessity, be in accordance with the trade qualifications and the unit requirements. In so far as aircrew trainees are concerned, enlistees are posted to the manning depot nearest to place of enlistment (except on such occasions as movements are effected to balance up deficiencies in recruiting considered in relation to training school intakes), from manning depots to schools in accordance with routing plan devised to synchronize with training requirements, with personnel proceeding in all instances to the nearest unit designed to accept them in the next stage of training.
The member for Hastings South (Mr. Stokes) asked whether we pay the same cost of living bonus as civilian employers.
No. Cost of living bonus to civilian employees of dominion government is governed by order in council PC. 6702 dated 26th August, 1941. According to terms of order in council P.C. 6702 dated 26th August, 1941, and treasury board interpretation of September 6, 1941, any increase in basic rate authorized since August 1. 1939, is to be deducted from the cost-of-living bonus; therefore, any employee whose basic rate of pay has been increased sufficiently will receive no cost of living bonus, whereas those whose rate has not been increased will still receive bonus.
Was that by order in council, or was it an interpretation by the treasury board?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: It was an interpretation by the treasury board of September 6, 1941.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
The specific case
referred to by the hon. member will be considered and further information will be brought down.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The same answer is given to the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) with reference to Calgary. At least, I fancy it is the same answer. If this ruling of the treasury board is to be accepted, then all I can do is to make further representations on the basis of what has been said in this house, and you may win.

War Appropriation-Air Services

Does the minister know whether it is possible for us to get some report as to the nature of the treasury board's interpretation and the reason for the decision arrived at, in order that we may try to persuade them to change their mind?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The discussions in the house will indicate to anyone who is at all interested that the general opinion in this house is that the interpretation is a bad one. I will send copies of Hansard or pass on to them the representations made to me in the house. I do not say that the decision will be favourable, but I will do my best.

I agree with the minister that the decision of the treasury board was bad. It was so bad that, I believe, there was a conference between the departments and representatives of the civilian ser- , vices. In fact, the other day I read part of a letter I had received from one of the members of the treasury board. I do not recall the details now, but it is on Hansard. I think the situation is bad, where you have two services, one working for the government and the other in civilian occupations, and one receiving the cost-of-living bonus while the other does not. It is creating hard feeling among the men in the service, and they feel that they have a just claim. I am pleased to hear the minister say that he will take it up further with the treasury board and try to get them to change their minds. It is a most unfortunate situation and one which should be cleared up.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: There are four ministers on the treasury board, and they may have listened to what my hon. friends have been saying and have decided to change their minds.
Who are the ministers?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The acting leader of the government is one, the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Trade and Commerce, I believe.

The hon. member for Bow River has emphasized the unfairness of paying different rates for the same sort of work. Is it not also true that the basic rate varies as between different places? The hon. member for Cape Breton South referred to a rate of 43| cents for general labour in the maritimes. The basic rate in Winnipeg at one time was 40 cents and I believe is now 45 cents.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I am informed that the Department of Labour sets this rate. Let us say it costs more to live in Winnipeg than in Prince Edward Island. Would my hon. friend

say the basic rate in Prince Edward Island should be the same as in Winnipeg, or should it not? I am just asking the question.
Would not the cost of living bonus enter into it?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not know; I am just asking the question. I am not trying to justify it.

Treasury board consists only of members of the cabinet, but they have certain advisers who sit with them. I should like to know the names of those gentlemen who sit with the treasury board1; I think that would be interesting to the committee and to the country. May we have the names of those who sit with and advise treasury board?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Really it is so long since I had the honour of being a member of treasury board that I do not remember the name of the secretary. I am told it is Mr. Ronson.

I think we would all like to know who are the gentlemen who advise the treasury board, because this seems to be a sort of super-cabinet; they seem to be able to make interpretations and decisions that do not coincide with what the House of Commons expects or, indeed, with what some of the ministers seem to expect.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is true.
I should like to know who the advisers are.
I think it would be well if we could learn also the names of those who are the advisers to the advisers of the treasury board.

A moment ago the minister asked me a question. In turn I would ask him if he would find out on what basis the different rates are determined, whether it is on the basis of a difference in the cost of living or whether it is on the basis of the going rates in the various parts of the country. Naturally I have no interest in seeing the rate at Winnipeg reduced to what it may be in the east, but it seems to me the difference should be explained, at least.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I really think these questions are more for the Department of Labour than for my department, but I am quite willing to make inquiries and see if I can get the information. At the moment I cannot give the answer because frankly I do not know why there should be a difference between the rates of pay in certain sections of the country. It may be based on the cost of living or what

War Appropriation-Air Services
have you, but I shall be only too glad to inquire and give the answer to-night if I can get it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The minister did not raise a point of order, but I listened attentively to the last few questions and I believe they are out of order. The Minister of National Defence for Air cannot be expected to answer questions pertaining to the Department of Labour.

This is not a question for the Department of Labour, because it has been under consideration by the Royal Canadian Air Force for the past year, so far as my end of it is concerned. There is a difference in the rates; I have gone into the question to a certain extent with the people in the maritimes and I understand that the rates are fixed by National Defence, without regard to any other department, based upon the prevailing rates in the district.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is right.

There is a difference as between different sections of the province. If they come in with a fixed rate and the district rate is lower, their rates are automatically lowered to conform to the highest local rate.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It is what I think they call the prevailing rates of pay.
That is right. What is in dispute so far as I am concerned is the cost of living bonus. At the moment I am satisfied with the minister's answer.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence

The hon. member for Cape Breton South asked the Minister of National Defence a question with regard to travelling allowances, berths and meals between eastern and western Canada. While this question was not put to the Minister of National Defence for Air, the answer has been prepared by him. Present regulations regarding rail transportation, sleeping car accommodation, meals and the like in connection with the movement of personnel as laid down in F.R.I. part 13, article 209, were put into effect, after careful study and consultation with the army, and the regulations of both services are uniform in this regard.
These regulations provide that airmen below the rank of sergeant, when travelling on duty, are entitled to second-class transportation and necessary meals. If the trip is of such duration that personnel are required to spend two consecutive nights or more on continuous journey they may be provided with berths in tourist cars, if available.
[Mr. Marshall.1
Because of the present train service in effect on Canadian railways there are bound to be some inconsistencies. The instance quoted to the effect that personnel from the maritimes destined to No. 1 manning depot at Toronto did not get berths is correct. Such personnel would actually spend only one night on the train. Personnel from points, Winnipeg and west, destined to No. 1 manning depot at Toronto are compelled to spend two nights on the train, and are therefore provided with berths in tourist cars, if available.
Furthermore, personnel moving between units in western Canada, for instance from Winnipeg to Edmonton, would not be provided with berths, since the journey involves only one night on the train. In this regard they are treated similarly to personnel from the maritimes to Toronto.
The statement to the effect that there have been cases of personnel travelling between Halifax and Montreal who have not been provided with meals is difficult to reconcile, unless they were proceeding on leave, in which case the onus for obtaining transportation and meals en route is the responsibility of personnel concerned.
The further statement that cases have occurred where personnel did not even get seats on trains between Montreal and Toronto is difficult to check. This may have occurred during a week-end rush, when the situation complained of was not peculiar to service personnel only.

I have some complaints
along these lines. In my opinion the joker in the arrangement is the words, "if possible." There should be no misunderstanding when a number of men in the air force are moved from place to place, on call of duty. That is not a decision made overnight. Those in charge of the situation must know they have a certain number of personnel who will be moving from- point to point at a certain time. The railway company should be so informed, so that they would have sufficient time to guarantee that men coming from Halifax to Toronto would be provided with the accommodation stipulated in the regulations.
It was a considerable group of men-I believe it was five, although I cannot vouch for it-that moved from Halifax to Toronto. They were not provided with meals or sleeper accommodation, and they spent two nights on the train. The last night on the train from Montreal to Toronto it was so crowded they had to stand most of the way. These were recruits being sent from Halifax to Toronto to take

War Appropriation-Air Services
basic training. That was not a very pleasant introduction to the service. Even then, they did not complain until they reached Toronto, and were told that they had been given a raw deal, and that personnel moving west of Toronto for the same purposes were provided with berths and meals. Evidently service on that end of the line is good. These boys had a specific complaint. I am sure their complaints were sincere, because I know some of them personally.
In my opinion the expression, "if possible," is the one which should be eliminated. There should not be any misunderstanding. If anyone has to stand up or go without a berth on a train it should be the civilian, who can travel at his own convenience, when he is not under pressure. The services are required to move on order, and there should not be any interference with the regulations concerning their comforts and conveniences en route.

A complaint has come to me repeatedly-I am sure other members have heard the same thing-which I should like the minister to clear up, because I believe it would be a good thing from the point of view of the general public. speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
When an aircraft completes a normal training or operational flight, the tanks are refilled, not drained, in readiness for the next flight.
Gasoline is drained from aircraft tanks prior to major repair and overhaul or transfer (when not under its own power), immediately after a crash and, normally, before being placed in storage. When gasoline is drained, it is returned to bulk storage or directly into refuelling tenders for re-issue to aircraft (when taken
72537-215}
from undamaged tanks) or filtered, mixed with lead free gasoline and used as M.T. gasoline (when taken from damaged tanks).
Gasoline removed from tanks of aircraft flown into a civilian contractor's plant for repair and overhaul is drained into the contractor's tanks (or into R.C.A.F. tanks where such exist) and re-issued to the aircraft on completion of repair or used for engine test purposes.

It is the unanimous opinion of petroleum technicians associated with national research council that the employment of re-refined oil in aircraft engines in Canada is not advisable at the present time.
While reclaimed oil is so used in the R.A.F., this is done for economic reasons which do not apply in Canada. In the United Kingdom, initial cost of oil is considerably greater; costs of collection and transportation are much lower, owing to shorter distances, and the volume of oil to be reclaimed is large enough to justify installation of the necessary machinery.
A large proportion of the used oil in Nos. 2 and 4 Training Command is being re-refined by a civilian company at Camsack, Sask., and returned for use in R.C.A.F. M.T. vehicles. There is no suitable contractor in the east, but the possibility of installing a plant in the Ottawa district, to be operated by the Royal Canadian Air Force, is being investigated. Such a plant, if installed, would serve Nos. 1 and 3 training commands.
The larger oil companies (who own practically all the oil drums used in the R.C.A.F.) are not particularly interested in purchasing used oil as an economic proposition, and the greatest difficulty is encountered in finding containers for accumulation of used oil for shipment to such smaller plants as are willing to accept it for reclamation. The small companies cannot supply drums and the large concerns require their prompt return owing to the war-time shortage of metals.
Reclamation of oil must be done to rigid specifications, under proper control. The experience of the army has shown that unit reclamation plants cannot be operated satisfactorily with the type of personnel available.
In the Royal Canadian Air Force as a whole, the only possible course at present is to dispose of used oil under contracts at the best prices obtainable. During the past nine months, 183,904 gallons have been sold for $10,515.09 -an average price of 5'7 cents per gallon.
