There was one on Laurier avenue at the air cadet place for three or four months; it may still be there. We supply the cadets with obsolescent craft so that they will know something about them.
Will the minister tell us whether the department has made any purchases of helicopters, or whether it intends to do so?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I think there are six, or sixteen, on order. I do not know when we are going to get them.
The minister has to buy them from the United States or Britain?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The United States.
Will they be equipped to alight on water as well as on land?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I think so. They are the latest type. But I do not know when they will be delivered. The R.C.A.F. have ordered a certain number of themi every year. I cannot give the hon. member offhand the delivery dates, and I doubt if you can be always sure of delivery dates on machines which are constantly changing. They are putting on new gadgets all the time.
Oh, yes; they are entirely different from the old gyrocopters. I was wondering about their capacity to land on water because I understand it is desired to use them for rescue work.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Probably.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Carried?
No, Mr. Chairman. This is the third largest item in the whole R.C.A.F. estimates. Does this include aircraft and engines for hemisphere operational work, only?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
It includes only Canada, not anything overseas. Overseas comes under item 13, $303,000,000.

War Appropriation-Air Services
The minister has given us the number of aircraft in the joint training plan.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I have not given it exactly. I said, 10,000 plus.
Has the minister had satisfaction with aircraft and things like, for instance, the Jacobs engine? I believe there was some trouble at the beginning.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not know of any engine or aircraft which has not been a headache at some time or other. Apparently the Jacobs engine is working pretty well now. There have been troubles with it. I know my hon. friend will not expect me to relate the technical details or to know what is wrong with piston rings or things like that. It was troublesome for a while, but I believe they Rave got what they call the "bugs" out of it.
Is the department buying gliders and transports for troops?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: We did purchase some gliders but they have not been very satisfactory. We have them in Canada. We have given or sold or leased some to the United States. The kind of glider we bought is not fully developed. We bought them from Great Britain; I could not tell the hon. member how many there were.
It will be necessary to have transports to carry paratroops?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes.

There is no air-borne
training being done in Canada at the present time?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Not by us. It would be an army job, anyway.
Yes, but the minister's department would have to provide the aircraft. We have a number of new heavy transport planes that could be used for air-borne troops, but they are not actually being trained.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: They are not actually being carried.
What company is supplying the helicopters, and what do they cost?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I shall have to find that out. As I said a moment .ago, these things are changing so rapidly that I do not suppose we would even have a fixed price for them.
Do you order them before you know the price?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Oh, you would, with a thing like that. We would say, "We want helicopters"; we would ask, "How much is it?" and they would say, "We don't know. We have to make this or that change. We will charge you the actual cost-plus," or whatever it is. Very often you do not know the price of equipment which is bought, because it is constantly changing; so that you cannot get a fixed price. I will try to find out. I suppose they give us a figure of some kind, but it would not be the actual figure until the thing is delivered.
Can the minister find out the carrying capacity? I think it is definite.

Will the minister give an outline of procedure with regard to overhaul work done on R.C.A.F. aircraft as regards what they have in their own repair depots and what they do by letting contracts to civilian firms?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Most of the overhaul is done by civilian contractors, but we have five or six repair depots of our own where we do ordinary repairs. The larger and more important repairs are done by civilian contractors.
That would be under the Minister of Munitions and Supply?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Yes. The companies are
almost crown companies. He has supplied capital to a great many of them. There is a firm of Macdonald Bros, in Winnipeg who were largely assisted with government funds. They have large hangars and aerodromes and facilities there. A good part of that was supplied by Munitions and Supply. I do not know how they figure the capital cost into the cost of overhaul. That is worked out between Munitions and Supply and themselves.
The ministers' department has nothing to do with setting the charges or the amounts to be paid for overhaul?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is entirely Munitions and Supply.
These figures have to do with home defence and not overseas?
Not overseas at all.
Not connected with overseas?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No.

(Peterborough West): I
thought some of these transports carried runways for emergency fields.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence

Does this include the storage fuel, oil containers and necessary equipment of that sort?

speechtext:
Fuel oil would be under operating expenses of properties.
Mr. MARSHALL. I am talking about the storage facilities of fuel oil, gasoline tanks. Perhaps if the minister would give us a break-down of the $26,000,000 we could find out.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I will furnish that to-night.

Is there any shortage of gasoline barrels or oil barrels to take care of the oil they have there?
Mr. P0W7ER: From what I read into the record, there is apparently a shortage of steel drums. The smaller companies have none to spare and the larger ones want to keep theirs for themselves.
Would the R.C.A.F. possess these for themselves if they had the opportunity?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: We have no drums of our own.

Would the department buy any, supposing the public had some to sell? There are quite a number of gasoline barrels and oil storage barrels throughout the country. Would the R.C.A.F. purchase them and keep them as their own?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: If we felt the need of these drums we would apply to the Minister of Munitions and Supply and he would get them. He is our contractor. We do not buy or order anything. If we want anything we ask Munitions and Supply who are our contractors.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: You do not buy directly, but you order them?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
We ask them to buy what our technical officers think is required. But
whether we are going to buy drums or not, I cannot say. If the technical officers say that we require something we ask Munitions and Supply,
They would ask if they were short of barrels, and I take it from what the minister says that they are not short of storage barrels?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not think we use them at all.
These machine guns are purely for Canadian use?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Absolutely.
Could the minister give a break-down of the $26,623,160?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes, we will try to have that to-night.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I suggest that the minister had better be prepared at eight o'clock to give a fairly comprehensive resume of the position with respect to these training contracts. There must be a good many of them covering various schools.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The hon. member for Lake Centre told us all about them the other day. As my hon. friend knows, he is more familiar with that than almost anyone else in the house. I will give what details I have. Does my hon. friend want to know how much each civilian club received?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not wTant to put the minister to unnecessary trouble.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It is easy; it is in the book.

I will put all that on Hansard.

speechtext: That was Sea island, but it is closed down now. It is used as an operational station.
That should not be called Vancouver, because it is in the riding of New Westminster.

It certainly is; that is why it was put there.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Peterborough West asked for a break-down of the next item. I am not trying to say that we

have passed this one, but I had better give him the break-down immediately, and I shall send it over to him.
I believe the minister was to give some information with regard to oil reclamation and the handling of oil, and he thought he would have it at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I thought I could getut, but I am afraid the officer in charge has not been able to give me the information. I shall have it during the evening or in the morning.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle asked if there was a separate gasoline contract for each individual school. All schools using Turner valley gasoline have individual contracts. Schools receiving their supplies under lease-lend are allocated their aviation requirements from the major oil companies as proportioned by the oil controller.
The hon. member for York West asked what percentage of leaded gasoline is used. All aviation gasoline used by the R.C.A.F. is leaded. The same hon. member asked whether cracked gasoline of 100 octane is used. No cracked 100 octane gasoline is used by the R.C.A.F.
The hon. member means none of the 100 octane gasoline is used in Canada?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
It is used, but not refined in Canada.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle asked how many gallons of oil were re-refined at [DOT] Kamsack, Saskatchewan, and the name of the company doing the work. The Northern Petroleum Company of Kamsack, Saskatchewan is a privately owned company, and the R.C.A.F. has no knowledge of its output.
The hon. member for Bow River asked if the department had looked into the question of reclaiming oil, and not selling it. He asked if it would not be worth while for the R.C.A.F. to have reclaiming machinery of its own. The air force has made a constant study, since the spring of 1941, with regard to the possibility of reclaiming used aviation oil for re-use in aircraft engines. We have been unsuccessful in locating a unit of equipment which will reclaim such oil to the satisfaction of the rigid specifications set up by our engineering division for re-use in aerial engines.
The study has recently shown a new unit, known as Refinoil, manufactured in the United States, which indicates that it may

War Appropriation-Air Services
be possible to reclaim aviation oil for re-use in Canadian transport, on an economical basis. Purchase of one unit has been approved for installation in the Ottawa district, for this purpose.
The hon. member for Battle River asked how much used oil is sold altogether. The answer is 209,726 gallons, for which the sum of $10,236.75 was received. This covers the period from April 1, 1942, to March 31, 1943.
The hon. member for St. John-Albert asked what percentage of oil can be reclaimed. The answer is that approximately eighty-five per cent can be reclaimed.
I understand from what the minister has said that the only plant for this refining is that at Kamsack, and that there is no plant in eastern Canada.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Correct.

Does that mean that Kamsack has brought used oil a considerable
distance?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
No; as my colleague has said, we are now thinking of setting up a plant in eastern Canada, in the Ottawa district. But so far we have not done so.
Mr. STIRLfNG: Does the oil at Kamsack come from territory from Winnipeg to the coast?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I would say probably all
of No. 2 and No. 4 commands, which would be as far as the Rocky mountains.

Very costly in freight,
is it not?

It would be, yes. But
there are concentrated in Saskatchewan and Alberta many of our training schools. I think they would all go into Kamsack, but it would not be economical to ship it east. We would have to have a plant of our own in the east, and that is what we are thinking of setting up. That would probably take everything from Fort William to Montreal. For instance, it would not be economical to ship from Mont Joli to Ottawa.

I was shown through an
aviation repair plant in the east end of London, Ontario. The gentleman showing me through the plant said that such-and-such equipment was for purifying oil.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I do not think we have a
plant there.

It may have been for
trucks.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
There was a very large
plant there for trucks and motor vehicles coming from Windsor. There was storage at that point. But we are talking about the refining of oil, and I do not know of any such plant in London, Ontario. There is an army plant, and it has nothing to do with us. They ship motor vehicles from Windsor, and store them in London. I believe it was a big building in connection with the exhibition grounds.

In the east end of
London?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
As a matter of fact I think
they took over the whole exhibition grounds, and stored motor vehicles there for several months.
They have the exhibition grounds, but the plant I have in mind is north of that. On second thought, however, I remember it was not for aeroplanes, but rather for army trucks and equipment.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes; that is correct.

Can the minister give
the quantity of aero-engine oil used from April 1, 1942 to March 31, 1943?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I can get that information,
although I have not it just now.

The minister has
given us the figures of the amount of oil sold by the air force between those dates, and I should like to have figures showing the amount used in the same period.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It can be produced.
I understand the minister will have a report to make later this evening or to-morrow morning. Can he get those figures?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I shall do my best.

13.	Overseas squadrons and ancillary units, $303,783,729.

The
minister supplied me a summary of costs overseas. I thought when I saw it first it was a break-down of the $303,783,729, but I find it is a break-down of the expenses of the air force overseas, including civil salaries, pay and allowances, gasoline and oil, laundry and the like- This is not the break-down I wanted because the $303,783,729 is not broken down at all.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
No; this was a deal we made with the British government whereby we pay

War Appropriation-Air Services
for all our squadrons overseas. This includes food, dental and medical stores and supplies, the purchase and maintenance of aircraft, and all other cost of the squadron. The expense depends upon the type of squadron. If it is a fighter squadron, it costs a little less to buy aircraft than if it is a bomber squadron. I do not wish to give figures, but I would suggest that, say, a Lancaster would be worth around a quarter of a million dollars. We pay for all that. Of course the figure of a quarter of a million dollars is just a rough guess. On the other hand a Spitfire would be in the neighbourhood of possibly $40,000 or $45,000. Payment is made on the basis of so much per squadron overseas per annum.
It is paid to the British government?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes, to the British government.
And these other expenses, on top of that?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes. I believe the actual cost of the squadrons to us is this $303,783,729.
But when we add up the other total it comes to $383,277,800.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Correct.
I notice an item here of $15,000 for photographic equipment. I should consider that very small.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: This is for overseas headquarters only. Everything we get overseas is paid for in this lump sum of $303,783,729. There is a break-down, but I suppose most of it is secret.
It fits into the other item, does it?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes. For instance for security reasons I cannot tell my hon. friend how many people we have overseas, but the pay and allowances for all our troops over there would come under this item,
Would the minister explain the great difference between the estimate for 1942-43 and that for 1943-44?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Before answering the hon. member may I add something to what I said to the hon. member for Peterborough West, because I believe I made a mistake when replying to him? The pay and allowances go into the first item, No. 2 on the list, for pay and allowances. So that the $303,783,729 does not include pay and allowances.
	.
Now, in answer to the hon. member for Vancouver East: Recently, in the month of April, we undertook to pay for all our troops overseas. Originally the men who went over were paid by the R.A.F. at R.A.F. rates of pay, and Canada made up the difference between the R.A.F. and the R.C.A.F. rates. We have now taken over the whole thing and are paying all our men the full Canadian rates. This runs into a considerable amount of money and it accounts for the difference the hon. member has mentioned.
That would appear in item 2?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It goes into item 2.
What about the clothing for these men?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Food and everything else are paid for on a per capita basis and is included in the $303,000,000. Clothing is on a per capita basis and is included under item 5. Item 13 covers medical and dental attention and everything else.
In other words, item 5, personnel supplies and services, does not cover the men overseas?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The $303,000:000 includes what is paid to the British government for feeding and1 everything else for our men overseas excepting clothing and pay.
We do not ship the clothing over?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The army does, but the air force does not.
The British government are responsible for clothing and feeding the men?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: At so much per head.
What is the rate?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not think that has been finally settled, although it is a matter of discussion between the two governments. The $303,000,000 is made up by estimating what it will cost to keep the men in the R.C.A.F. squadrons in England for a year. I do not think the rate for the last war has been settled, but at that time they paid something like $2 per man per month.
It will be most important that someone find out some time.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
They were still working on the rate for the last war ten years ago, and I do not know what settlement eventually was made. I think they arrived at one on a

War Appropriation-Air Services
hit-or-miss basis and decided to call it square because Canada owed them so much. I imagine that is what will happen in this war.
Surely the minister does not mean $2 per man per month?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Per day. That covers food and clothing and ammunition, if it is an infantry man.
From the very' beginning Canada paid the pay and allowances and upkeep of her army overseas, but we have done this only recently in connection with our air force. Why was that?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Under the empire training agreement Canada undertook the responsibility of paying practically all costs in Canada, which amounted to eighty per cent of the total cost. Great Britain undertook to take the man from the moment he got on the boat at Saint John or Halifax or any other eastern port and pay him from then on. Canada undertook to pay the difference between the British and the Canadian rates of pay, because the British rates were somewhat lower. In April of this year we signed a new agreement whereby we become responsible for the pay and allowances of all the R.C.A.F.
Is the difference in pay between the R.A.F. and the R.C.A.F. rates made up to the man who has joined the R.A.F.?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Who joined the R.A.F.
pre-war?
Yes.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: If a man joined pre-war, he would probably still be R.A.F. The hon. member for York-Sunbury referred to one man who went over in a cattle-boat. We would not be paying the difference in pay to a man who is still R.A.F.
He cannot get transferred back to Canada to the R.C.A.F.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
That has been a matter of great discussion. The man to whom my hon. friend has referred could apply to his commanding officer for transfer to the R.C.A.F. If his commanding officer recommends it and we find that he will be useful to us, we would take him in. There have been only two or three cases of transfers because it is a very difficult matter. Take a man like Collishaw, who is now air vice-marshal. If he were transferred, there would be a matter of seniority to consider. The matter of transfer from the R.A.F. to the R.C.A.F. is rather difficult.
* Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury): I know of another case of a man from Canada who went overseas pre-war and joined up with the R.A.F. He became a very useful man and was sent to Canada for instructional purposes, still with the R.A.F. He has not been allowed to transfer to the R.C.A.F., although I have been trying to get him transferred.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: He could make application to his commanding officer.
He has made application and they do not seem to want to let him go. This man could be very useful to Canada.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The difficulty is that the more valuable a man is to the R.A.F., the less they want to transfer him to the R.C.A.F. That is one of the difficulties. The R.A.F. do not want to send back the good men; they may send us a lot of fellows who are not so good.
I am still trying to get him transferred.

The
minister has said that clothing and equipment are included in the $303,000,000, but there is an item here in this list of the R.C.A.F. overseas war establishment estimates for clothing and necessaries, $2,615,909. Would that be for men who are not really in the war establishment overseas?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am advised that clothing is in another item altogether.
This item of $2,615,909 is exactly the same as it was last year.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That would be under item 5, "personnel supplies and services: food, medical supplies and services, clothing and personal equipment." That is how my hon. friend gets the $3S3,000,000 instead of the $303,000,000. The cash amount we are going to spend on the squadrons is $303,000,000.
The $303,000,000 will have added to it the other figures in here?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Absolutely.
Then there is a small item of $12,355 for medical supplies and services.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
That would go into the
$383,000,000; that would be for headquarters' personnel.

Perhaps the other figures are also headquarters?

War Appropriation-Air Services

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes.
Would it not be wise to place this table on Hansard in order that it might be available to other hon. members.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I would be glad to make this available to my hon. friend personally.
Mr. M&cINNIS: Is the Canadian government paying all the expenses in regard to the empire training plan in spite of the fact that we are taking care of our own men overseas?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence

speechtext: Does Canada pay the other part?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The actual cash is spent by Canada; then Britain owes us that much.
Do New Zealand and Australia pay any part of the expenses?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The cost is divided half and half between Britain and Canada, and then Australia and New Zealand pay Britain so much per head.

Does the minister mean that the total cost of the air training scheme is cut in half; that Canada pays half and Britain the other half, and that Britain then charges Australia and New Zealand so much per head for training their airmen?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is quite right. That is to say, in the agreement the cost up to 1945 was fixed at roughly $1,400,000,000; Great Britain undertook to pay through lease-lend or in kind, $723,000,000 approximately and Australia and New Zealand then make their own arrangements with Britain either through credits or some other system.
They pay so much per head to Great Britain?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Yes, the reason being that Canadian pupils constitute roughly fifty per cent and pupils from Britain, Australia and New Zealand the other fifty per cent. But Britain has the right to send us Netherlanders or men of any other race, provided they keep within the quota of fifty per cent. They may

send Poles, Norwegians, Netherlanders up to Britain's quota of fifty per cent, and they are charged to Britain's share.
Mr. ADAMSO'N: Are our squadrons overseas paid for on a per diem basis? The expenses of a squadron might vary considerably depending upon the number of operations undertaken, the losses in operation and many other factors. Is it a fixed sum per squadron per diem, or what?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence

speechtext: Do we estimate the maintenance at the beginning of the year, or does that depend on our losses?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Under the arrangements made with Britain in January the capital cost of the latest equipment is $74,000,000 and the annual maintenance cost of the latest equipment is $222,874,000.

That is an all-Canadian
squadron?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No; for the authorized Canadian squadrons.
And that is irrespective of the number of operations in which it is engaged? It is a figure arrived at empirically?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It is mostly guess work, subject to review every year.
It is an empirical figure?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes.
Who pays for the establishment from which the squadrons operate- the hangars, the buildings, the administrative structures? Does Great Britain pay that, or does it come out of this item?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am advised that we make a lump sum payment and the Royal Air Force pay everything else. It goes into the per capita cost. Suppose we have a group headquarters in the north of England and have to take over a castle or a house or something of that kind. That goes into the cost per squadron.

Suppose another hangar is wanted at such and such an aerodrome? Britain puts it up and'-

War Appropriation-Air Services

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
That goes into the cost of the squadron. The Royal Air Force pay for it originally and charge the accommodation back to us.
Mr. MaoNICOL: When item 9 was under discussion the minister said that gasoline for overseas use would come under item 13, if any. May I ask whether the gasoline used in the planes flown by Canadian pilots over* seas is supplied by Great Britain or Canada?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is what is called the ferry command. That is Royal Air Force.
No; I mean planes flying from England to attack Germany or Italy.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is charged in this
Is it supplied by Britain?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes, and paid for under this per capita system.
The gasoline used over there is 100 octane, is it not?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I should think so.

The British and the
Americans all use 100 octane gas. The axis powers, I have read, have not been able to develop the 100 octane gas, although they have invented a process whereby they get over S7 octane. German gasoline is a good deal higher than 87 octane; it may be well up to 100, and I have been wondering just what would happen if German planes were transported across the ocean either in submarines or by some other method and came in contact with our aeroplanes on the Atlantic coast.- If the Germans were using a gasoline close to 100 octane, their planes would be much faster because 100 octane gas drives the planes faster; they can also climb more quickly and carry a heavier load. A four-motored bomber, with four 1,500-horsepower engines, using 100 octane gas would carry five more 1,000-pound bombs than a plane could that was using 87 octane gas. I am just wondering what our planes on the Atlantic coast would do if attacked by German planes using this higher octane gas.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I would not be able to answer the somewhat involved technical question put by my hon. friend, but I do know that all our ships flying from Canada to Britain use 100 octane gas.
That is the bombers on the ferry command?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: All the planes used in our coastal operations would use 100 octane gas.
But this afternoon the minister said a lower octane rating was used.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I was speaking of training planes. They would not necessarily use the 100 octane gas, but our operational planes would.
That gives me a good deal of relief if our Atlantic coast planes are using 100 octane gas.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: What my hon. friend has in mind probably are the planes flying on the northwest transport stage.

No; I was thinking of our planes flying on the Atlantic coast.
Mr. POW'ER: They would all use 100 octane gas. I thought my hon. friend had in mind the planes on the northwest stage route that goes up north to Alaska. They are mostly American planes, carry American gasoline of 100 octane rating. I do not want to go into particulars, but the C47 and the Lodestar, for instance, both American planes, use 100 octane gas, like all American planes.
All the gas used in the United States war planes is 100 octane. We make no 100 octane gas in Canada?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not think so.
I hope after we win the war Canada will see to it that we get some of those vast boilers which the Germans use in the hydrogenation process to assist in making high octane gas.

A few moments ago the minister was answering questions relating to the transfer of Canadians in the R.A.F. to the R.C.A.F. He left us rather up in the air, and I am still wondering if there is not something his department could do on behalf of Canadians who are anxious to make such [DOT] a transfer. As he knows, there are cases of men-I have been in touch with the minister about one-

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
That has been under very active consideration and still is a matter of discussion with the Royal Air Force. The R.A.F., very naturally, do not want to lose some of their best men. Some of their men who joined before the war, say five or six years ago, have the natural feeling, now that we have a Royal Canadian Air Force that they would like to join us. They have first to go before their commanding officer. If he gives permission we check up on the applicant, and if he is suitable for our purposes we take him in. But so far the thing is still only being discussed.

War Appropriation-Air Services

I fully understand the position of the Royal Air Force in that situation, but it seems to me that as yet the , machinery is not very clear. The minister says that a Canadian in the R.A.F. who wishes transfer to the R.C.A.F. can go to his commanding officer; that is. I take it, to his commanding officer in the Royal Air Force. I have in mind a case of a Canadian, who- incidentally, he served in the last war-joined the R.A.F. before the R.C.A.F. was over there, and is now in Canada. He was posted to Canada at his own request because of the difficulties his family were facing under the lesser allowance, and he finds now that he is likely to be posted back to Britain. While he is perfectly happy to go back he would like to go back in the R.C.A.F. He tells me that he approached the R.A.F. commanding officer, and that that commanding officer told him to get in touch with the R.C.A.F. at Ottawa. He has been in touch with me, and I have taken the matter up with the minister, who has given me by letter the same reply he made this evening. There seems to be no other move which can be made; the man is stymied whichever way he turns.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The thing is in process of being settled. It is not settled yet. But the man to whom my hon. friend refers would not be suffering from lack of pay, because even if he is R.A.F., if he is in Canada he gets paid at R.CA.F. rates of pay. Does my hon. friend understand that?

I understand that perfectly. The point is that he expects to be posted back to Britain very shortly, and that if he is then in the R.A.F. his family's allowance will be reduced, whereas if he were transferred to the R.C.A.F. before being posted back, that would not happen.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: My hon. friend is quite right. That is one of the things we are trying to settle.
The minister will agree with me that this man faces quite a difficult situation.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Quite.

I wonder if the minister has in hand a statement of the approximate number of gallons of gasoline that were used, say last year, or the number estimated to be used under this appropriation, by our air force overseas-

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
My hon. friend wants to
know how much gasoline we use in our training schools in Canada?

How many million
barrels?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: My hon. friend wants the figures of consumption in Canada, does he? I would not know what was being used by our squadrons in Britain. If my hon. friend wants to know how much gasoline is used in our training schools in Canada I will try to get that for him.

I should like a compilation of the amount of gasoline Canada is using in- all its war activities. I am not in a hurry to have the figures to-night. Would the minister give the number of barrels, and the octane content, first in- Canada, then the number used on the sea-coasts in the defence of Canada, and also the number we pay England for, in the flying of our air service overseas?

As to the first two matters
for which my hon. friend is asking, what we are using in training, I think I can get for him; then, what we call home war establishment on both coasts, I think I can give him that too; but I doubt very much whether the British government would let me know how many gallons of gasoline they use in our squadrons over there.

I wondered how this
estimate was made up. Would the minister not have some record from the British government of how many gallons of gasoline they call upon us to supply to fly our machines overseas?

If the minister is
getting that information as regards gasoline, I wonder if he would couple it with the amount of motor oil-lubricating oil for machines-used in Canada.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I think we can get that.
Does the same agreement apply to Canadians in parts of the world other than England?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: In Ceylon and-?
Africa.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Absolutely.

How about ground
crew? The other night the minister was discussing the relative numbers of Canadians in the Canadian squadrons and Canadians in the R.A.F. squadrons. The Canadian squadrons now have Canadian ground crew. Are there any Canadian ground crew with R.A.F. squadrons, or are there any Canadian ground crew in other parts of the world than Great Britain?

War Appropriation-Air Services

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
We have something like
5,000 radio mechanics who are in the R.A.F. all over the world. They are ground crew; they are not flyers.

Are .they considered
ground crew?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes. They do not fly. They are not aircrew.
No; they do not fly, but I did not know that they are definitely considered as ground crew. One more thing: There is no formation in Canada corresponding to the R.A.F. regiment?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No.
We have no such unit for aerodrome protection?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The army does that for us.
It is mostly veterans' guard.

Referring to the
matter of Canadians serving in the R.A.F., I wonder if there is any sufficient reason why Canada should not undertake to pay Canadians who are serving with the R.A.F. such an amount as, added to what they are receiving from the R.A.F., would put them on a basis equal to that enjoyed by those serving in the R.C.A.F. -

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
We do that; all Canadians
who enlisted in the R.C.AT. originally and are overseas, whether they be in Burma or India or Ceylon, are being paid Canadian rates of pay. The only question is that of men from Canada who before the war went to England and joined the R.A.F. They never were R.C.A.F.; they joined the R.A.F. and still belong to it.

But they are
Canadians.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
They were born in Canada; they are Canadians. But the question becomes more and more complicated. If you go back twenty-five or thirty years you will recall that quite a large number of men-Collishaw, for instance-who were in the Royal Air Force, remained with it after the war. I doubt very much whether these people want to come to the Royal Canadian Air Force, and if they did I do not know just how they would fit in our picture if they are senior to many of our people. But the ordinary man who left here before the war-a great many of them went over in cattle-boats and the like because they were in a hurry to join up-can make application to his commanding officer, and if the commanding officer-who is Royal Air Force- approves it we will accept it. As, however, I
told my hon. friend, the question is not quite settled ; there are all kinds of difficulties about it. The man who enlists in the Royal Air Force joins for six years; with us in the Royal Canadian Air Force he joins for the duration of the war. The Royal Air Force would have the right to say to us, "This man has joined for six years. If you take him into the Royal Canadian Air Force, will you pay him for the services he does not render us?" The pension rates have been fixed by the Minister of Pensions and National Health and next-of-kin of the men would be paid at the Canadian rates of pension. If they left four years before the war they are on Canadian rates of pension. The only question for them is, do they want to come to the Royal Canadian Air Force. If they do we are most sympathetic, but we cannot buy them out of their contract with the Royal Air Force.
Although they are on Canadian rates of pension, the British government has to pay the pension?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes; that is to say, if they have a disability when they come back; or if unfortunately they are killed, their widows or mothers, or whoever the next-of-kin may be, will be on Canadian rates of pension.
Paid by the British government?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Paid by the Canadian government.
The Canadian government?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The British pay according to their rates and we make up the difference.

May I press further the case of the family of the man to whom I referred a few minutes ago. This man is one of those who got over to Britain probably on a cattle-boat before the Royal Canadian Air Force got there. He was a Canadian, with a home and a family in Canada. He went to join the Royal Air Force and is still in the Royal Air Force. While he was in England his family in Canada received allowances less than those received by dependents of Royal Canadian Air Force men, but he was posted to Canada and is here now and the allowance paid his family has been increased. When, however, as is quite likely, he is posted back to England in the near future, the allowance- received by his family will go down again. ,

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is so.

If it is possible for extra payment to be made to the family of this

War Appropriation-Air Services
Canadian in the R.A.F. while he is in Canada, why is it not possible for that same extra amount to be paid to a Canadian in the R.A.F. in England?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The hon. member states the case accurately; what he has said is quite true. I do not know, however, why the Canadian government should be charged with the payment of extra rates for somebody who is not serving this government. He is serving the British government.
Who pays the difference between the British and the Canadian rates while this man is posted in Canada?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The Canadian government does.
Then one might ask, why should the government do that? If the government does that while the man is in Canada, why not do it for him while he is in England?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am advised that he is a servant of the air training plan and that a part of his salary would be charged to Great Britain. We pay the whole lot and Britain pays its share to us. That is the only way I can explain it.
He is serving this government.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: While he is here he is serving this government. When he goes back to England he is not serving this government and I do not know what justification there would be for us to pay extra to his wife or next-of-kin when he is no longer our servant.
While he is in this country he is serving this government, and yet the minister is not in a position to make representations on the man's behalf in his endeavour to be transferred.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I could make representations, but I very much fear the British government would not listen to them. If this committee thinks that we should pay somebody who is serving some other government, that is a different matter. As I have told1 my hon. friend, this is one of the thorny points we have to discuss and decide. We could transfer him to the R.C.A.F. if the British government would allow him to be transferred, but they think he is too valuable.
He is their enlisted man.

I can see that the problem is thorny if you try to force the R.A.F. to

allow the man to transfer to the R.C.A.F., but it is not quite so thorny to consider paying the dependents of a Canadian, when he is in England, just as you do when he is here. I wonder whether that point has been given consideration.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am advised that we have made representations. If we want to pay R.C.A.F. dependents' allowances to all wives and next-of-kin-New Zealanders, Australians and everyone else-of men who serve in Canada, the other governments would not like to undertake that financial obligation. It is too much. They do not want to take it on. The R.A.F. have fixed their own rates and they do not see why they should pay Canadian rates.

At the moment I am not suggesting that you should try to get the R.A.F. to increase its rates. I am suggesting, however, that the Canadian government, which pays the difference to the dependents of a Canadian while he is located in Canada, should also consider paying that difference to the dependents of a Canadian while he is posted in England.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I will look into the matter. I am serious about it when I say that I do not know how it can be done. After all, he is working for another government. He may be a Canadian, but he hired himself to another government. Why, therefore, should we pay him the difference between our rates and the salary which he contracted to take, including his dependents' allowance and what have you? If the Canadian people wish to do it I have no objection. Perhaps my hon. friend can make a good case.
It is tough on the dependents here.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes; but why should we take over responsibilities that are not ours? We are not getting service for it from the man in question.

Does it not rather weaken the minister's argument when you reflect on what he said a few minutes ago? If this man, a Canadian in the R.A.F., is unfortunately killed overseas, this government will accept responsibility-

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: My hon. friend has me there.

-for dependents' allowance, in addition to the British dependents' allowance, although he was not this government's responsibility and was not serving them. This government, nevertheless,

War Appropriation-Air Services
have agreed to pay that difference. It is a very good idea, but if you carry the argument to its logical conclusion it weakens the minister's argument.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I fear my hon. friend has me there; he is logical and I was not. It is the Minister of Pensions and National Health, with his well-known sympathetic consideration, who has put it over for the pensions. The position is most illogical, but it exists.

Just what is the difference between your paying these boys the difference between the English and the Canadian standards and paying the R.C.A.F. boys who are serving the R.A.F. as you do? What is the material difference?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not quite understand that.
We pay the Canadian boys who are now serving in the R.A.F.-

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Right.
-because they belong to the R.C.A.F., and we make up the difference?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes.
So far as their contribution is concerned, where is there any difference?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: None.
Is it not all the same cause?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The only answer is that one contracted with the Canadian government and the other with the British government.
But it is all the same cause.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I agree with my hon. friend and I have been trying to work it out, but I have not yet done so. If the committee will let me struggle with it again we may succeed.

May I make a further comment in connection with the minister's struggle. The man who joined the R.A.F., when he is over here in Canada, is rendering us a service, the minister says, and therefore we are liable for him. If you are to be consistent you should say that the man in the R.C.A.F. serving with the R.A.F. should not be our responsibility. I do not want the minister to adopt that principle, but it is logical. It seems to me that if we still maintain responsibility for those who are with the R.A.F. when they are here in Canada, it
is perfectly consistent for us to accept responsibility for Canadians who are with the R.A.F. over on the other side.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Perhaps I did not make myself clear. If the man is serving in Canada in the empire training plan, it is the plan that is responsible for him while here, though Canada is the administrator of the plan. Britain pays fifty per cent of the cost, so that he is charged to the plan and Canada only pays fifty per cent of the increased pay and allowances. Then when he goes back to Great Britain, as my hon. friend suggests he is on R.A.F. rates of pay; he is not on the Canadian rates or the B.C.A.T.P. rates. Then he is working for the British government, not for us. I do not mind studying the point further, but I am convinced that it would not be logical for us to pay his salary and allowances any more than it would be logical for us to pay a share of the salary of the colonial secretary, say, or anything else. It is true, of course, that we are fighting for the same cause.
As the hon. member for Weyburn says, it is just as logical as what is being done by the Minister of Pensions and National Health.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Yes; we have done an
illogical thing in taking responsibility for the man's pension.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
