The
information bureau sends it out?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The casualty list; not Wings.
Where is that edited?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: At our headquarters here in the Jackson building. We have a printing establishment of our own, and we sell this paper for five cents. It is rather a good looking publication.

What is the cost of
operating it?

Does it pay for itself?

War Appropriation-Air Services

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not know but it must come pretty close to it. We do not carry any advertising in it, so that the revenue cornea from sales at five cents per copy.
Does it carry any af the speeches in this house?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No.
How is the increase of $3,000,000 made up?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Does my hon. friend want a break-down of these sundries?

A break-down of the
additional amount. How is the increase made
up?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: There are four items I have here: photographic equipment, printing and stationery, air cadet expenses and air cadet capitation grant, and sundries. There is a sum provided under B.CA.T.P. for photographic equipment.
That is for taking photographs from the planes?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: This amount in item 14 includes such things as public relations, photographs of our airmen and so on. We have a little procedure of our own; if unfortunately a man is killed we like to be able to send a photograph to his next-of-kin.
It does not mean the equipment used to take photographs from planes?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No.
Does that include the photographing of the letters of airmen which are sent by air mail, the airgraph letters?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No; those come under the Post Office Department.

The minister has not
given any figures in regard to recruiting. What item do they come under?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: They are in here.
What is the cost of recruiting?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
It comes under the sundries;
I will get it. The total cost of advertising recruiting campaigns last year was $340,000. The total anticipated for this year is $750,000. That covers radio, advertising and all the things that go with recruiting.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not think so. I think principally we are publishing half-page advertisements in the metropolitan dailies and that sort of thing. It costs quite a lot for a half-page advertisement.
And of course this includes the recruiting for the women's division?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes. We are now looking principally for aircrew.
Could the minister give some explanation as to the rapid increase in the cost of recruiting, some general explanation?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Any explanation would only be this, that a year ago it was very easy for us to get aircrew; they were flocking into our recruiting depots, but now it is becoming tougher to get aircrew and we have to go out and look for them. At one time we really had too many; now we may be running short, though not very much.
Could the minister give any particulars as to any new means or methods that are being employed in connection with recruiting, which would bring about this increase in cost?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: By full-page or half-page advertisements in the newspapers; by radio talks; by moving pictures; by any sort of stimulation that would make the younger generation want to join the air force. We have the air cadet league and all these things which go to make people feel that they would like to join the air force, and what we really need are aircrew.
Then the minister would say there is no new method of recruiting but rather a general expansion of the old methods?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes.
Is the cost of the air cadet movement included under this item?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes. Expenses last year in connection with the air cadet league were $1,100,000, and the air cadet capitation grant- that is to say, we pay so much for the clothing of the air cadets-came to $20,000 last year and is estimated at $35,000 this year. We expect fifteen thousand more air cadets.

Are many transfers accepted from the army into the air force

War Appropriation-Air Services
ground crew? I am thinking of a number of men who have sought to be transferred from the army to the ground crew of the air force. Is there much of that being done?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I would not think so; certainly not at the moment. A man has to get permission from his commanding officer before he can transfer, or rather he must get his discharge from the army and be reenlisted in the air force, and that is rather difficult.

To get back to the question of advertising, all over the country to-day we see large photographs which look like lithographed pictures in colour. As I go down the main street of my own town I see three or four of these large photographs in each store window. To me they look like costly photographs, and I should like the minister to tell us approximately the cost of each one. It seems to me this is a great waste of money. Surely we should be able to advertise the air force to better effect than through these pretty pictures, especially when we see three or four of them stuck in a small store window in a small town. I have had a great many people complain to me of the extravagance shown by scattering so many of these pictures around the country.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I would have to find out the cost. The problem of recruiting is, I suppose, like the problem facing a tobacco company, say, that wants to sell its cigarettes. It constantly impresses upon the public that its cigarette is much better than any other. That is what a company does when it wants to sell tooth-paste, and so on.
And are you trying to show that the air force is better than any other service?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Therefore the air force has these pictures, but I could not tell my hon. friend what they cost per sheet.
They are very extravagantlooking pictures.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes, they are very extravagant-looking. And the reason why we want to make them extravagant-looking is that we want to make people say they want to join the air force.

Is this advertising, socalled, done through recognized commercial advertising agencies? Is the advertising placed through that sort of medium, or is it done directly by the air force through posters in the * newspapers?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I think it is done through
advertising agencies, usually. There is one
in Toronto, I believe-Cockfield, Brown and Company. I am not sure of the name, but anyway there is one. In fact I think all the advertising agencies have got together now to carry most of the government advertising.
I believe that organization is known as National Advertising. There has been an amalgamation anyway. I would not really know the name of the firm that carries our advertising, because it is all mixed up together.

The thing which amazes me is that when the minister rises in his place to talk about his methods of recruiting he refers to the cost of advertising. It boils down to this, that the one of the three armed services which can do the best advertising gets the recruits. I can just imagine that when the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services is before the committee, and we ask him. how he gets his men, he will say it is done by advertising. He will say that they have to go out and advertise, and that they have to advertise a little more attractively than does the Minister of National Defence for Air.
Therefore, in the final analysis, the fellow who makes a profit out of this thing is the advertising man. I must say the whole method is wrong.

Is there any cooperation among the three armed services in the matter of going after recruits? I am wondering where national selective service enters into the picture. According to the minister's story, this is a matter of competition between each department to see who can put on the best show, to get the men. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I would not exactly say
that. As a matter of fact the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services says he does not have to advertise for the navy, because it has an appeal of its own. * For many months we in the air force did not have to advertise, either. But at this time we shall have to advertise, if we want to get the people we want. And I am not in competition with the Minister of National Defence, army, because we have a different class of people we take. Possibly I should not put that on Hansard-I should say not a better class.
Better put a soft-pedal on that.
National selective service does not help you, at all?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
They would not help in
connection with the people we want. We want aircrew, and you cannot conscript men

War Appropriation-Air Services
to fly an aeroplane. They have to be either natural fliers, or volunteer for duty, because in no place in the world, so far as I know, have they had conscription for aircrew.

I agree with that, entirely; but the young boy who leaves school, and is reaching his callable age, might go to the national selective service and say, "I am about to be called." The selective service man might say, "You had better hop around to an air force recruiting station, because you are a pretty bright-looking lad." Then he might say to the other fellow, "You had better wait until you are called up, because you are not so bright." One fellow is turned away because he may be none too bright, and the bright fellow goes into the air force.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I was not going to say exactly that, but that is about the truth of it.

The minister has said he cannot conscript these people to fly. I am satisfied that many of the best men in the aircrew overseas have been chaps who in the early days of the war received their call, or were conscripted in Canada. But they decided they were going to join the air force.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Perhaps my hon. friend is right, in respect of many cases.

If the young men called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act were given some time after they were called to volunteer for air force or ground crew the minister would not have to advertise for recruits. He would not have to advertise if he -were given that choice of going into the air force after they were called up for military service. He could take his pick of all he wanted.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I think when they are called up they are supposed to report to the army centre. But before they report they can come in and report to the air force.
And they do.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: And they volunteer for air force. Many of our ground crew have been called up. But there are not so many in connection with aircrew, because they are mostly younger men. Our aircrew now are nearly all under twenty-one years of age. Originally we took them up to thirty-two years, but that class is now pretty well exhausted. We are taking them between eighteen and twenty-two.

Is it possible, in respect of a young man who is anticipating a call-up probably in a year or six months, to take him on strength and give him 'leave to continue in

his civilian occupation until such time as the air force requires him to report for duty. It has come to my attention at least on one or two occasions that it is possible for a young man to come to an air force recruiting station, be sworn on strength, taken into the force and then given indefinite leave for maybe three or four or five months, before being required to report for service, and in that way he avoids being taken into the army in the regular way.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That was .the custom about a year ago. Since March, 1941, in connection with applications for enlistment as aircrew, men enlisted in the R.C.A.F. immediately upon application, even though some period might elapse before they could actually commence their training. In those days we had more than we knew what to do with. But now they might get a month or two months. A man might enlist to-day, and we would say, "Come back on July 15." They do not get more than a month.

He is
actually on. strength, though, when he does enlist?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes, and he is paid one dollar when he is sworn in.
He is a dollar-a-year man.
If he were discharged, and the question of pension arose, would the Minister of Pensions and National Health say he was not in the air force?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: My hon. friend asked that question the other day. Immediately the applicant completed his enlistment he would become an airman and, as such, would be subject to air force law, and to the proper orders of superior air force authority. His leave of absence could therefore be terminated at any time by directing him to report for duty. During the period of leave of absence *without pay, however, he would not be liable to perform any air force duties, and in consequence, in the event of his being injured or killed during that time no claim for pension would arise because the same would not be based upon an injury received arising out of the .performance of an air force duty.

My point was in connection with an enlisted man who was sent home for a month on leave, without pay-or just a dollar, as the minister indicated. He did not contract the sickness at that time, but contracted it after he was

War Appropriation-Air Services
called up again and was placed on duty under the R.C.A.F. It was then that the question of pension came up. They said,, "You were not enlisted. You were not in the force at that time, and we can only count you in the force, so far as pension is concerned, from the time you were recalled." That is my point.
I say that when he came back, after being called the second time, he was actually on the force from the day he first enlisted. He contracted the illness after the second call, and his pension should begin from the time he actually enlisted.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: My hon. friend is referring to the Sommerville case.
Yes.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am having it looked into. That is really a pension case, rather than an air force case, because, after all, once a man is discharged from the air force, his .pension must be handled by the Minister of Pensions and National Health.
I agree with the minister on that, namely, that it is really a pension case.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes.

But it is also a matter of principle. If, after a man is called up the second time, an illness occurs, for purposes of pension he should be considered as having been on the force from the day he was sworn in, not from the day he received his second call-up. That is a matter of principle which should be cleared up. I am glad the minister is looking into the other case.

I was going to ask a further question along the lines of one I asked a few days ago. I have just forgotten what answer the minister made with respect to the fleet air arm. We have not a fleet air arm here. But the British are recruiting in Canada, are they not? How are our young	men	being enlisted	here	and sent
overseas?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
My hon. friend the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services says he does not	think they	are.	I do	not know,really.	There may be	some who	are beingenlisted in the fleet air arm of the Royal Navy,	but	I cannot	say,	from	my own
knowledge.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Not now.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The minister says it is not being done now.

I do know about this, because just a few days ago a young friend of mine went overseas, to England. He was only nineteen years of age. He went to the fleet air arm, and it is my understanding that someone here in Canada induced him to join up, and to enter that branch of the service. Of course he may have wanted to go; but how did he get into the fleet air arm? How are they enlisting?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not know how to answer my hon. friend. I am trying to get all the recruits I can for the Royal Canadian Air Force. I really would not know how they are getting recruits for the fleet air arm. The Minister of National Defence for Naval Services says he does not think they are doing it. But if my hon. friend has a case in mind, then it must be done. There is nothing to stop its being done. But there is no encouragement by way of financial assistance being given by the Canadian government to people who are enlisting in the fleet air arm. That is the best answer I can give.

Early this year I had a call from two men who had joined the R.C.A.F. in January, and were told to report some time in 'March. They were given a card which instructed them to tell their employers that they had signed up, but to continue with their jobs. They told their employers, and they were immediately given notice that they would be through at the end of the week or at the end of the following week. They then had two months to put in before they would join the air force. I immediately took the matter up with the minister's department and these boys were called earlier, but this might happen in other cases where boys might be left out on a limb until they were taken into the force. I think these men should be warned that when they tell their employers they should watch out and let the air force know if they are fired from their jobs.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: At the present time I doubt if there is more than one month from the time they actually sign on until they are called in.
In this case it was over two months.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: In January we had a surplus; now we are running into a shortage, but we expect to have a surplus in June or July.

Following up the matter referred to by the hon. member for Daven-

, War Appropriation-Air Services
port, is it not a fact that when a man in Canada who is not subject to call under national selective service wishes to go overseas to join the fleet air arm or the ferry command he must first get a permit from the Department of Labour, and that the Department of Labour will not issue such permit unless it is concurred in by the air force?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I never heard of any such rule. It may exist, but the question has never come up. In the early days or before the war a great many young Canadians went overseas to join the R.A.F., but since the war, since they have had the opportunity of joining the R.C,A.F., very few have gone over.
I was referring to men who might not be qualified for pilots' positions in the air force and who are not subject to military call.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: If a man wants to join the ferry command he must be a pilot or a navigator or an observer and would have to be trained unless he was a former bush pilot.

I am referring to men who have paid for their own tuition at flying schools and who might be above the age limit permitted by the R^C.A.F. I have known of one or two cases, and I wonder if this is the government policy?
Is there not some establishment of the fleet air arm attached to certain stations in Canada?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Under a contract with the British admiralty we are training airmen at Kingston for the fleet air arm, but they all come from the other side. An elementary school will be opened in October; Kingston has been in operation for over a year, and there is another in Nova Scotia. These men train under the British commonwealth air training plan, but they go to the British navy. They come from Great Britain; they are not recruited in Canada, but they receive their full training here.
I know of several young men who had passed the university school with the highest honours, and they were sent overseas almost immediately^.
Since this is the last item, perhaps the minister will tell us when we may expect answers to questions which have been asked, but which have not yet been answered.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I shall have to check
Hansard. I shall be only too glad to ask my colleague to answer them on the opening of the house to-morrow. There are a great many

questions that will have to be looked up, but we will put the answers on Hansard.
I am particularly interested in one I asked with reference to the average rate of wages paid to civilian employees in various classifications and which appears on page 3251 of Hansard.

I do not want to block my own estimates, but I have a duty to perform. I made a statement on Thursday on commissioning, and the high commissioner for Great Britain wants me to correct any impression I may have left in the minds of hon. members. Therefore, I should like to read into Hansard a letter which he wrote me, as follows;
Dear Mr. Power:
In the course of your speech on air force commissioning in the House of Commons on the 2nd of June, you stated the Royal Air Force policy to be that an arbitrary figure of fifty per cent of graduates from training schools, namely thirty-three per cent on graduation and seventeen per cent after service in the field, were commissionable, and no more. This would mean that the R.A.F. had established 50 per cent as a rigid maximum of all pilots, observers, navigators and air bombers who could receive commissions.
That is not the case. The policy is that all members of aircrews of the above categories who qualify for commissions shall be commissioned, although the Royal Air Force view is that not more than about half of aircrew posts need to be filled by commissioned officers. It is also true that experience has shown that no more than 50 per cent qualify for commissions in practice. For this reason it was decided that some 33 per cent should be eligible for commissions on graduation, whilst a further 17 per cent should be recommended for commissions after a period of operational service. But these percentages do not exhaust the opportunities of commissioning, since the Air Ministry are always prepared to consider any number of additional recommendations on the strength of operational records. Whilst the suitability of a certain proportion of pupils for commissions can he clearly recognized at the stage of graduation from training schools, the R.A.F. feel that the test of the qualities of the others cannot really be satisfactory except in actual operations. No commanding officer of any squadron in the R.A.F. has then any limit placed upon the number of recommendations that he can make. On the contrary, he is encouraged to recommend any pilot, observer, navigator or air bomber who possesses the necessary qualities of leadership and command.
This policy was affirmed clearly during^ the Ottawa conference in May last year, and it is not qualified by any question of rigidity in the matter of establishment or any other consideration except the qualifications of the individual.
The Royal Canadian Air Force have adopted their own policy. They have as much right as the R.A.F. to adopt whatever policy they consider best, and the R.A.F. are cooperating fully in the implementing of that policy so far as

War Appropriation-Naval Services
Canadian personnel are concerned. This is only one example of the spirit of comradeship in which our air forces are operating together against the enemy.
That means in reality that you would not be embarrassing the Royal Air Force by granting commissions to more than fifty per cent.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Exactly.

It is now some thirteen months since I ments in the press or by radio to the
presented the last estimates of the Department of Naval Services. Much has happened in those months. We have undertaken certain new duties; we have continued and enlarged upon some old tasks. We have had some brilliant successes; we have had some tragic losses. But on all these matters a great deal has already been said through the medium of speeches, interviews with the press and state-
Canadian public. Therefore I doubt whether I can enlighten the committee to-day by presenting any new material. I can only hope to survey events that are already for the most part well known, to bring together in what I trust will be convenient form information that in one way or another is already, I am sure, in the minds of hon. members.

War Appropriation-Naval Services
The story which I have to tell, Mr. Chairman, is in the main a story of progress, progress in the size of our navy, both in ships and in man-power, and now, I have to add, woman-power as well. When we began to build up a navy some three and a half years ago we were young to the task. Except for a few officers and men we lacked experience. We have learned something in the hard school of war, and while it would be vain to say that we are beyond the range of criticism; while it would be foolish to assert that we have not made mistakes, we can say, I think, that we have performed our duties with some credit to this country, and certainly we can state that we have won the approval and the praise of many authorities on naval matters in other countries.
"Where the treasure is, there is the heart also." The treasure of a navy is its ships, and the heart of a navy is its men. I shall speak first of these precious and vital elements in our naval story. I shall then tell the committee something about the operations in which the Canadian navy has engaged itself. My remarks on these three topics must necessarily be general, but further detailed discussion can be had as the individual items of the estimates are under consideration.
Ships. When I first spoke to the house in November, 1940, I pointed out that at the outbreak of war the Canadian navy had some fifteen ships but that, even as I spoke, the number had grown to 155 ships of all classes. Each succeeding year since then has seen more ships built and commissioned) than we had estimated. For instance, in the last fiscal year we planned to add about 100 ships to our strength. As a matter of fact, we added over 150. To-day the Canadian navy boasts a fleet of over 550 ships of all types.
That is a remarkable rise from the little fleet of fifteen with which we began the war. It represents a 36-fold increase.
During the last year two Tribal destroyers were completed for the Canadian government in British shipbuilding yards. Two more of the same type will shortly be completed and commissioned in the same yards; and two more steel are under construction in a Canadian shipj'ard.
Tribal destroyers belong to the largest and most powerful type of destroyer in the world. It has been and it is our feeling that these ships should see service as fleet destroyers rather than as escort destroyers, and we have made arrangements with the United Kingdom authorities to that end. The two Tribals already in commission, the Iroquois and Athabaskan, are serving with the British fleet,

and the others as they are completed will join the first two. Thus eventually we shall have a Canadian flotilla of Tribal destroyers assigned for service with the British fleet and manned by Canadian officers and men.
I am glad to be able to report that the Royal Navy has in its turn placed four of its own escort destroyers at our disposal, and these destroyers have become part of the Canadian convoy escort service in the north Atlantic. These four destroyers have been renamed, according to our policy of naming destroyers of this type after Canadian rivers. We have given to these ships the well known names of Ottawa, Gatineau, Kootenay and Saskatchewan.
You have not Carleton there?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
It is possible that before the end of the year the British navy will be able to give us two more escort destroyers.
This gift by the British navy is very highly appreciated, and these destroyers will be of the greatest service to the Canadian government in its escort work on the Atlantic.
While the figures which I have given as to the increase in the number of ships are matters of gratification to the Canadian naval service, they speak eloquently of the work that has been done by Canadian shipyards, and in the factories and foundries where the steel and the machinery and the other materials required by these shipyards are manufactured. In the years immediately before the war, shipbuilding in Canada was practically nonexistent. Last year the tonnage of ships built, that is both merchant ships and warships would aggregate about one million tons, and this year that figure will be greatly exceeded. I think we can say now that Canada is becoming a naval and a maritime power.
Our facilities for the training of men have been developed to a point where we are now able to man the ships which are available to us. The task has been difficult, I am bound to say, but we have always been able to keep the manning of ships abreast of construction, so that our ships are not kept out of operational duties through lack of trained personnel.
Men. I now come, Mr. Chairman, to the question of men. We began this war with an active service personnel of 1,774 men. At the end of the last fiscal year, that is on March 31, 1942, our personnel had grown to

War Appropriation-Naval Services
31.000,	and it was our plan to take men into the service last year at the rate of about 1,000 a month.'
Now in the case of personnel, as in the matter of ships, we have far exceeded our estimate. In the year that has passed we took in about twice as many men as we had planned to take. To-day the man-power of the Canadian navy stands at approximately
60.000.
We have doubled our size in the last fourteen months. We have increased our stature thirty-four times since the outbreak of war.
That is a rate of expansion not paralleled, I believe, in all naval history. An article in. the March issue of the British magazine Shipping described it as an all-time record. On the list of the .navies of the British commonwealth we stand second-second only to the British navy itself.
If we maintain the rate of growth which we now contemplate we shall by the end of next year reach approximately the number of men that the British navy had in prewar days. We shall have about 90,000 men.
I am sure that if, in the early days of September, 1939, anyone in this chamber had predicted that the Canadian navy would some time in 1944 have as many men as the British navy had before the war, he would be branded as a visionary of the wildest sort. Yet his vision will soon be justified. For there is no dearth of recruits for the Canadian navy. In fact, we still have a waiting list at some of our naval volunteer reserve divisions.
The men of the Canadian navy come from every part of Canada, and a few from beyond our borders. I should like to place on Hansard a table showing naval enlistments by provinces, complete to the 31st of March of this year:

Some 1,400 of our officers and men are serving with the Royal Navy in widespread parts of the world. About 20,000 are serving in Canadian ships; the others are training at shore establishments.
Training. I come now to training. The training of our naval ratings is normally undertaken in one or the other of four ways. First, at Royal Canadian Navy Volunteer Reserve divisions of which there are eighteen throughout Canada, beginning with the division at Charlottetown in the east and ending at Vancouver in the west. Second, at our naval bases and training schools, of which we have seventeen. Third, in technical schools and universities, and fourth, in our ships.
It requires about six months' training for a man to qualify for the lowest rating. It takes about fourteen months to train fully a naval artisan. Stokers, engine room artificers, electricians, radio artificers, shipwright welders, motor mechanics, coppersmiths, boilermakers- these are some of the trades which have to be known and used in a modern navy. Stewards, cooks, supply assistants, waiters, also need' training. Then we need gunners, torpedo men, asdic operators, men who understand the intricacies of radio direction finding, or R. D. F. as it is commonly called. We need also men who are skilled in the art of communication, who understand wireless, and visual signalling, coding and decoding.
A modem ship of war is in itself an intricate bit of machinery, and its operation requires skill, not merely in seamanship, but in a great variety of other trades as well.
The training of officers is now done at King's College, Halifax, and at Royal Roads, B.C. After an officer has completed successfully his training there, and has spent some time at sea, he may be given further courses of trainring ashore at H.M.C.S. King's or elsewhere, depending upon the specialty for which he wishes to qualify.
Early this year a new scheme for the entry of officers in the Royal Canadian Navy was adopted. In the first years of the war we followed the principle of what is known as "direct entry"; that is to say, a man could, if he was assumed to have the proper qualifications, enter into officer rank directly from civilian life. Concurrently with this system we also followed the practice of promoting promising men from the lower deck, and from the outbreak of war to the introduction of the new system, 1,086 ratings were promoted to officer rank in this way.
In February of this year we came to the decision that there should be no more direct entries into commissioned rank except in the special branches. All persons who wish to become executive officers in the naval service must enter the service as ordinary seamen and they must take at least six months' training as ratings. perhaps must be served at sea. If at the end of that six months' time a rating is considered worthy of a commission, he is commissioned as a probationary sub-lieutenant and he takes at King's the course of training laid1 down for such officers. This method of entry is new and has not been fully tested, but it is designed to put a premium on ability and adaptability to the requirements of the service.
In recent months we have made arrangements with several Canadian universities, and we hope to make arrangements with some more, for the establishment of what we call university naval training divisions. These divisions will correspond in a general way to the Canadian officers training corps establishments of the army. Preliminary instruction will be given during the academic year, and during the summer months a two weeks' training course will be provided on each coast. Students who enrol in these courses will be on divisional strength of the volunteer reserve division which is nearest to the university.^ I am happy to say that we received most satisfactory cooperation from the faculties of the universities in this matter, and we have also received much helpful advice and valuable assistance from the Canadian army through the units of the C.O.T.C. at the universities.
While on the subject of personnel, I should mention the fine work of the medical branch of the Royal Canadian Navy. We now have in that branch some 300 medical officers and 132 nursing sisters. Forty of our medical officers have been loaned to the Royal Navy, and many of these are seeing service with the ships of that navy in all parts of the world.
Since the outbreak of war the health of our personnel has been good; only three per cent of the days available for work have been lost through hospitalization. This represents a loss of less than ten days per man per year, and compares very favourably with the normal loss in industry. When we consider the difficult conditions under which our men often have to live at sea, the crowded living quarters, the exposure, the mental strain under which they labour, the incidence of a sickness is a matter of considerable satisfaction.
The naval medical research unit has continued to give careful study to the problem of suitable diet for men at sea, and it has made what I think are notable improvements in dietary conditions. It has also worked out an excellent type of emergency ration for lifeboats and rafts, and its improvements in this regard have won the attention and approval of naval medical men in other countries.
The studies which our medical research unit has made in rationing and in dietary problems,

generally, should prove of great benefit after the war when the problem of rehabilitating and restoring the health of the populations of the conquered countries arises. I am sure that the services of such men as Commander Best of this unit, famous throughout the world for his researches in the treatment of diabetes, and of his associates, would be of great value in the solution of post-war health and dietary problems.
Sea cadets. Under the subject of personnel I must make reference to the sea cadet movement. Of striking interest during the past year has been the great growth in the sea cadet movement in this country, and in this work the navy league of Canada has rendered enthusiastic and powerful assistance. The boys who have been trained as sea cadets provide one of the finest sources of recruits which the navy has, and we estimate that to-day more than 4,000 former sea cadets are enrolled in the Royal Canadian Navy or in the Canadian merchant navy.
When I spoke to the committee a year ago, I said that there were 2,700 sea cadets in Canada. To-day there are 61 sea cadet corps and the enrolled membership is, in round figures, 10,000. Summer camps have been established in different parts of the country, and it is hoped that the majority of the cadets will be able to attend these camps. Here they will receive training in elementary naval work, in the handling of boats, in swimming, and in discipline.
We have recently held training classes for the officers of the sea cadet corps in Halifax, in Toronto, in Victoria, and these classes were attended by 175 sea cadet officers. Apart altogether from the value of this work to the navy, I am glad to say that highly satisfactory and gratifying reports have been received from the parents of the boys and from law enforcement authorities who have watched the beneficial effects which sea cadet training has had in decreasing juvenile delinquency.
W.R.C.N.S. I pass on now to the Women's Royal Canadian Naval Service'. During the past year the Canadian naval service has begun to enlist women into the Wbmen's Royal Canadian Naval Service. These women are commonly referred to as "Wrens". We have now some 2,500 in this corps. The basic training for ratings is conducted at Galt, Ontario, at an institution made available to us through the generosity of that province. The training of Wren officers is carried on at Ottawa.
Generally speaking, the services performed by the Wrens will be domestic, administrative and clerical. I must say that those who

War Appropriation-Naval Services
have joined the corps have adapted themselves with great enthusiasm and efficiency to naval life and service conditions. They are-working as stewards, clerks, cooks, sail-makers, laundresses, drivers, telegraphists, stenographers, and in many other positions. Members of the corps are now to be found on duty in Halifax and Deep Brook, Nova Scotia; in Ottawa; in seven of the volunteer divisions throughout Canada; as well as on the Pacific coast.
Naval College. An event of high importance in the last year, and one that I hope will be of increasing significance in the years to come, was the opening of the Royal Canadian Naval College at Royal Roads, British Columbia, on Trafalgar day, October 21, 1942.
Some 300 Canadian -boys sought entrance to the institution, but the enrolment was limited to 100 students. Fifty of these, the older cadets, are taking a one-year course; fifty more have embarked on a two-year course. They come from every part of Canada, and they have been carefully selected not only on their scholastic qualifications, but also on a physical and personality basis. After they complete their work at the college these young men will undertake further training with the Canadian Navy or with the Royal Navy.
Operations. I pass on now to the third main part of this summary, namely, the part that deals with operations. The operations of the Canadian navy during the last year have taken its ships and its men to various points on the Pacific, to areas in the north and south Atlantic, and into the waters of the Mediterranean. Some of our ships have joined with United States forces in the waters of -the Aleutians, and some of them still stand on guard on our western seaboard. Seventeen of our corvettes saw service in the North African expedition. The Canadian corvettes Ville cle Quebec, Port Arthur and Regina definitely sank three enemy submarines and captured their crews, and other Canadian corvettes made promising attacks on submarines in that area. But our main work as a navy has been in the north Atlantic. It has lain in the protection of trade convoys, in- the guarding of merchant ships, carrying food and war supplies from the ports of this continent to the harbours of Europe.
From time to time, both before the outbreak of war and since, we have received much advice as to how oqr naval effort couldi be best directed. There were some who felt that the proper role of the Canadian navy lay in the establishment of a fleet of fast -motor-boats, presumably to guard our shores
against the attacks of enemy surface ships. There were and there still are others who claim that we should -have concentrated our efforts, at least in part, on the manning of cruisers, and still others who feel that we should have featured the building and operation of submarines.	.
It is true that there were several courses open to us at the outbreak of war. We could have attempted to man great ships, if we could have gotten the ships, such as battleships and heavy cruisers. These might find work to do in far away waters, but there would be very little scope for their activities in the seas that lie between America and Europe. Or, again wie -might have endeavoured to organize a fleet of motor-boats carrying torpedoes, or we might have attempted to form a submarine navy. These craft, too, would have to go far away from home to find work, for there were and there are few enemy surface ships in the open Atlantic. The British navy has seen to that.
But we chose another and, I believe, a truer and more natural course. We looked at our geographical position, at our great agricultural wealth and at our industrial possibilities. We knew that Canada would send across the seas not only thousands and -hundreds of thousands of fighting men, but huge quantities of food and munitions of war. We knew that enemy submarines would threaten the ships which were to carry those men and supplies from Canada to Europe. Indeed, we believed from our experience of the last war that enemy submarines would -be the greatest menace that our merchant ships and our troop ships would have to face.
That view, all too unfortunately, has proved correct. By almost unanimous agreement among spokesmen for Britain, the United States and Canada, the Atlantic is our first and major battle ground; it is there that the war against Hitler can be won or lost. And so we said in the Canadian navy: let us undertake the task that lies nearest to our hand. Let us build a fleet of escort vessels that will guard the lives of Canadian service men on their way to Europe, that will protect the products of Canadian farms and-Canadian factories on their long journey over the seas. That seemed to be a distinctively Canadian type of effort-a close-knit, compact effort, with most of the ships being built here, the men trained here, the work directed from here. While from time to time we have assumed other tasks, in other places, we have clung to our original design, and it is on the north Atlantic that our chief work as a navy has been done.

War Appropriation-Naval Services
Now, from the shores of this continent, over thirteen thousand vessels have sailed in convoy, carrying some eighty million tons of food and war supplies to the ports of the United Kingdom.
It must be admitted that in the early days our part in the Atlantic convoy system was small. We had at the beginning only six ships that were fit for the work. We had only a handful of men. We had to plan and to build and to train, and there is no more difficult task in all the preparation for warfare than the building up of a navy. The training of naval officers and petty officers takes time, much time. After all has been done on shore that can be done, officers and men still must have practical experience at sea. It takes time to rehabilitate shipyards and to build and equip ships. It takes time to construct ashore the facilities that are necessary to a navy-the docks, the wharves, the repair shops, the machine shops, the barracks, the training quarters for men. Bearing in mind the resources of the country in manpower, shipbuilding, ship repairing, and _ its possibilities as a training ground, our constant aim has been to develop a service that was properly balanced as to men, ships, training and shore facilities. Bit by bit we increased our strength and enriched our experience. From the small beginnings that I have already mentioned, we progressed step by step until last fall we were able to say that nearly one-half of the convoy escort work in the north Atlantic was being done by Canadian ships operated by Canadian officers and men.
The significance of that statement is worthy of most careful note. If the winning of the battle of the Atlantic is the first and most important of our tasks, surely it is significant that so large a share in the conduct of that battle has been entrusted to the Royal Canadian .Navy. Of equal significance is the fact that on the first day of May of this year a Canadian officer was given the important post of commander in chief of the Canadian northwest Atlantic. That appointment arose out of discussions between the service forces of Britain, the United States and Canada, culminating in a conference held in Washington in March of this year. As a result of these discussions, the whole responsibility of escorting convoys between these shores and the shores of Great Britain is now divided between the navies of the United Kingdom and Canada.
What is the name of that officer?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I am just coming to that. I am glad to be

able to say that in selecting an officer for this important post we felt we could place our confidence in a graduate of our own Canadian naval college, in a man who has seen distinguished service with both our navy and the Royal Navy,, Rear Admiral L. W. Murray, a Canadian, a Nova Scotian. He has operational control of all anti-submarine activity in the northwest Atlantic. Cooperating with him, working in the same building with him, is Air Vice-Marshal G. O. Johnson, who has been given control of all anti-submarine air activity in this area.
I am happy to say now that from the beginning the cooperation of the Royal Canadian Air Force and the Royal Canadian Navy has been close and complete. The new arrangement under which Rear Admiral Murray is made comipander in chief of the Canadian northwest Atlantic, and Air ViceMarshal Johnson is given control of the air command in that region, will mean that the resources at our command, in- the way of both surface ships and airships, will continue to be utilized to the best advantage and in the closest cooperation.
I cannot pass from this topic without recognizing the assistance we have received from the United States and Royal navies. Our friends in the United States have always been glad to make available to us their ship repair and supply facilities, and sometimes their ships. Their experience and information have always been cheerfully placed at our disposal, and their air patrols over the Atlantic have been and are most welcome and helpful. The Royal Navy, as always, continues to assist our efforts. This assistance is most felt in the free use that we have been allowed to make of their unrivalled training facilities, of their plans and designs for ships and machinery and armament. We are glad to be able to offer a measure of reciprocity and the Royal Navy is now making use of some of our training facilities in this country.
The battle against the submarine ebbs and flows as the tides of the sea. We have had months when our losses of merchant ships were heavier than we expected. There have been times when our losses were lighter than we had estimated.
Hon. members will recall that in 1917 the depredations of German submarines became highly alarming. Indeed, it is clear now that there was a period of time in that year when many authorities in. Great Britain feared that the war would be lost on the Atlantic. The sinking of merchant ships by German submarines had reached such proportions that many people in high places felt that if the

War Appropriation-Naval Services
rate of sinking were maintained, the supply of food and munitions of war from these shores to the ports of Great Britain would dwindle and fade to such small proportions that the United Kingdom would be starved into submission. But in that year Great Britain answered the German submarine threat by introducing the convoy system. Instead of letting ships put to sea individually, Britain adopted the policy of grouping them together and sending them out with fast armed surface craft to repel submarine attacks. It is a matter of record now that after the introduction of the convoy system the losses from enemy submarine action dropped sharply.
To-day Germany is again relying on submarine warfare. She has made, within the last few months, many boasts and many threats. But so far she has not produced any new type of weapon, any novel type of submarine. She is, it is true, building stronger submarines. They are more difficult to sink. They are more heavily armed. They are better equipped. They have more bases in Europe at which they can repair, refit and refuel.
They attack now in groups, instead of singly, but beyond those things no new styles in German submarines or in German methods have yet. come to our notice.
The exact number of submarines which the German navy has is known only to the Germans themselves. Undoubtedly the number is large, and their cruising range is long. We are often asked, "Where are the German submarine bases on this side of the Atlantic?" Many people think that German submarines must have some bases on this side of the ocean at which they can refuel and reprovision before starting on their homeward journey. All I can say in answer to this question is that if there are such bases on our coasts, we do not know of them. We do know, however, as I told the committee last year, that German submarines can leave their bases on the coast of Europe, make their way to the shores of Canada and the United States, operate against shipping for some time, and then return to their lairs without reprovisioning or refuelling.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister referred to "some time". What does he mean by that, in point of actual time?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I
would say two or three weeks, depending upon how much territory they wished to cover. But I should think two or three weeks would be quite within-their capacity.
Two or three weeks of operations.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Yes. In the last war German submarine bases were confined to German or Belgian territory. With the fall of France, Germany obtained bases farther to the west, and therefore nearer Canadian shores. She derived another advantage from her occupation of Norway, the low countries and France, namely that she could now establish submarine bases opening directly into the Atlantic, whereas in the last war her submarines, in order to operate against our shipping had to move out to the open sea, either through the English channel or ' through the North sea.
In consequence of these positional gains German submarines, even if they were only of the same type as were used in the last war, could operate much farther to the west. The result of all this was that the western Atlantic, which was practically immune from submarine attack in 1917, became in this war a very heavily infested submarine area. The fall of France was a heavy blow. In several respects it was nearly fatal to us. But in no way was it more serious than in its effect upon naval strategy. The whole Atlantic now became a submarine theatre. If the British navy, in addition to its tremendous tasks elsewhere, had to take on the added burden of protecting convoys in the waters off Canada and Newfoundland, the task would certainly have proved extremely difficult, if not indeed impossible.
It was in these months of late 1940, and in the months of 1941 that the Canadian navy, small though it was, filled the gap. In the words of Sir Percy Noble, spoken at Montreal in March of this year, "The Canadian navy sailed into the breach. The expansion of the Canadian navy solved the problem of Atlantic convoys". These are gratifying words from a man who during those difficult days, was admiral commanding the western approaches to Great Britain, and who probably knows more about convoy problems than any other living person.
It may be asked, "What is being done here and in Britain and in the United States to meet the submarine menace?" I should answer to that, in the first place, and to take events in their proper order, that the first effort of the united nations is to kill the serpent in the shell before he can be hatched. It is directed against enemy submarine bases and submarine building yards, and it takes the form of heavy air attack. The Royal Air Force, the American Air Force, and the Royal Canadian Air Force have made many such attacks, and there is no doubt that these attacks will have

War Appropriation-Naval Services
their effect. But we must remember that German U-boat bases are strongly built and strongly defended. Heavy concrete cover is provided and other forms of defence are adopted, which makes the task of our air men difficult.
In the second place, we are meeting the German submarine threat by building in Britain, in the United States and in Canada, more anti-submarine vessels, more destroyers, more frigates, more corvettes. Not only are we turning out more and more ships; we are endeavouring to improve the quality of our ships, to increase their speed and to strengthen their striking power.
But it is not only on ships alone that we rely in our battle against the submarines. The aeroplane has become a most important weapon in submarine warfare. I disclose no secret when I say that the convoy which is protected by both surface craft and aircraft is in a much happier position than the convoy which is protected by one type of craft alone. If you have aircraft protesting the convoy, submarines are not nearly so likely to expose themselves by coming to the surface, because a plane in the air can spot a submarine on the surface of the water far more readily than a vessel can and1 the plane can, of course, speed to the attack much more readily than can surface craft.
This war has shown the value of aircraft carriers to a fleet, and we have been giving careful consideration to the possibility of establishing a Canadian fleet air arm. We have had discussions on the point with our friends in the R.C.A.F., as well as with naval authorities in Britain and the United States.
There are many factors to be taken into account, of course, and all I can say at the moment is that we are continuing to give most careful study to the whole matter, but we have not come to a definite conclusion. One of our high ranking naval officers is now abroad for the purpose of seeing at first hand the operation of carriers and of fleet air arms generally.
The Atlantic ocean is very wide and there are parts of it where air coverage is difficult to get at all times, but I can say again, as I said before, that the cooperation between the ships of the sea and the ships of the air is thorough and wholehearted.
Without disclosing a definite figure I can say, too, that both on the sea and in the air we are considerably stronger than we were last 37ear. We have more ships, more planes, more men, more experience. Our coasts and coastal waters are more heavily defended and more ships are available for convoy escort work.

This year the Canadian navy hopes to add some seventy fighting ships to its strength, besides a number of other ships, not of the combat type. We shall dispose of these ships to the best possible advantage. Some of them' are to do transatlantic escort duty. Some of them will sweep up enemy mines, if such are sown along our coasts and shipping lanes. Others will patrol our coastal waters. The point to remember in connection with the protection of ships is that, as an English writer recently said, "The sea is one." If you have a sea lane to protect, you must protect all of it. It would be idle to mass all your protecting ships on one part of it and leave the rest of it unguarded. Naturally you put your strongest force where you expect the heaviest attacks. That is what we mean by saying that we shall dispose of our ships to the best advantage.
Last year the enemy penetrated the gulf of St. Lawrence and the lower reaches of the river and sank twenty allied ships in these waters. At that time the resources of the united nations at sea were strained to the utmost. This year a reasonable portion of our fleet is allocated to this theatre and the air protection is also stronger, so that we look on ourselves as reasonably well off in this area.
We are asked sometimes by cities or other communities whether we can guarantee that our defences are adequate, whether we can guarantee that certain localities are immune from attack. It is extremely difficult to give such guarantees. It is extremely difficult to say that under no circumstances whatever will enemy sea craft or enemy aircraft reach our shores at some point or other. Therefore, when a certain town or city or other locality asks for an assurance that nothing will ever happen to them, I find it very hard to give definite assurance.
I shall not attempt to say that we shall not have further losses at sea. Indeed, it is certain that even with our increased strength, and even if we became much stronger than we are to-day, or than we plan to be, we should still have losses. The U-boats lurking under the water, the floating or sunken mine, the enemy aircraft making a sudden thrust from the coast of Europe against our shipping lanes, the surface raider even, will continue to take their toll against our shipping.
At one time last year I made a calculation of the mileage of convoy routes which had to be protected by units of the British navy, and I estimated that 86,000 miles of sea lanes had to be guarded by that navy. When you add to that the great distances from the western coast of North America to the battle

War Appropriation-Naval Services
theatres of the southwest Pacific, or even to the Aleutians, you have an immensely long line over which troop ships and merchant ships have to be protected, and you can see how difficult it is to guarantee absolute safety to any ship over these great distances.
When I add to that statement the remark that on any given day there are at least two thousand British merchant ships on the sea, not to speak of the merchant ships of the other united nations, the magnitude of the problem of protecting allied merchant shipping becomes apparent to us all.
But yet, when I look at the shipping and the submarine problem as a whole, I see no cause for alarm. Doctor Goebbels, it is true, declared a few weeks ago that the U-boats had England by the throat. There is no evidence whatever to support the statement of the eminent doctor. The fact is that in the very month of April of this year when he spoke, more merchant ships reached England from North America than in any other month this year or last year. Second, allied merchant ship losses due to submarine action in the first five months of this year were considerably less than they were in the first five months of 1942. Exactly how much less I shall not say, but I use the word "considerably" with due regard for the meaning of language. Third, we have done very well this year in sinking submarines, better than we did in the same period of last year. Fourth, there is no doubt whatever that we are now building merchant ships faster than they are being sunk. I know that this fourth answer is not a complete answer, because in some of the sinkings, unfortunately, we lose some of those excellent merchant officers and seamen who have carried on under such arduous conditions with such magnificent gallantry for nearly four years.
Therefore, while the activities of U-boats still constitute a grave problem, and while we must never for an instant relax our vigilant pursuit of them, I have no doubt as to the outcome of the struggle on the Atlantic and on other seas. I have no doubt that in time our surface ships and our air ships will triumph in that struggle.
The Canadian navy is, as to more than ninety per cent of its strength, what might be termed a civilian navy. I pay deserved tribute to our professional sailors, the nucleus on which our strength was built. Without their experience and their training the organization of the Canadian naval service to its present proportions would have been impossible. But I must at the same time render my homage to the more than fifty thousand
men who have come from the ranks of the merchant service, or who have left the office, the farm, the fishing boat, the factory, the mine, the lumber camp, to join our ranks. They have quitted themselves like men and they have been strong.
Nearly one thousand men of the Royal Canadian Navy have already given their lives in this great struggle and twelve of our ships of war have been sunk. There is no sea of the world which is not hallowed as the last resting place of some of the best and bravest of our Canadian youth. They have died gallantly. They have died gloriously, and their memory will remain an inspiration to those who come after them in that service to which they gave their lives.
But they have not gone unavenged. Eight German submarines have been destroyed by Canadian ships of war. Many more have been damaged. Some more must be classed as "probably destroyed".
The heroism and the accomplishments of our men have been duly recognized. Their gallantry and devotion to duty have been rewarded by no fewer than 387 decorations and mentions in dispatches.
I have tried to give the committee in what must be rather factual and prosaic form a sketch of the Royal Canadian Navy and its work. I have only glimpsed the story. The full tale cannot be told until the veil of secrecy which necessarily surrounds so much of the navy's activities will be lifted at the conclusion of the war. He who would understand what this Canadian navy has done must himself go down to the sea in a ship. He must see for himself the hazards of convoy work, the trying weather conditions which our men have to face, whether they serve in the merchant marine or whether they fight under the white ensign. He must observe the gales, the high seas, the ice, the fog, the, constant threat of the elements that must be faced, as well as the ever-present risks of war. He must talk to the men of the sea as they come in from their voyages and as they go out again, knowing that every minute of every day, for weeks on end, they run the risk of disaster and death.
He must learn the story of young Day, of Belleville, Ontario, an ordinary telegraphist aboard the Canadian ship-of-war Otter, who, dying on a raft in the cold of the salt winter air and water, rallied his strength to encourage his shipmates with these last inspiring words, "There'll always be an England".
He must hear sailors tell of the time when Commander Hibbard of the Canadian destroyer Skeena remained on the bridge of his

War Appropriation-Naval Services
ship for sixty-six hours in midwinter, fighting off a bitter submarine attack on his convoy, and brought his ship safely into a United Kingdom port. For that act of enduring gallantry and for other consistently good work Commander Hibbard was rewarded with the Distinguished Service Cross.
He should listen to the story of Lieutenant Keefer, an Ottawa boy, who, when his ship was engaged in picking up survivors of a torpedoed Norwegian craft, leaped into the water to rescue a Norwegian woman and gave his own life in the endeavour to save the life of another. For his heroism he was awarded posthumously the Albert Medal and the Norwegian Medal of St. Olav, the latter being the highest award in the gift of the Norwegian government.
He ought to hear the tale of the coolness and courage of Petty Officer Bernays, of the Canadian destroyer Assinibome who, in a battle with a German submarine, held to his post in the wheelhouse while flames lighted by German shells leaped around him, and while enemy bullets whistled close to him. For more than thirty minutes he stood at his wheel, receiving and executing in that time no fewer than one hundred and thirty-three helm orders and enjoying at the end the satisfaction of seeing the German submarine disappear, a broken hulk, beneath the waves, and her officers and crew captives aboard his own ship. For his superbly gallant conduct he received one of the rarest awards, the Conspicuous Gallantry Medal.
The exploits of these men and of many others like them are the stuff of which great traditions are made. These are the men who are writing indelibly the name of Canada on that great scroll -which records the gallantry of the men of the sea.
Mr. Chairman, with every confidence, I put the record of the Royal Canadian Navy and the request for the moneys necessary to carry on its work before the committee and the house.

Mr. Chairman, the statement made by the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services about the work of his department and the activities of the Royal Canadian Navy has been a rather short one compared with those which were made by the Minister of National Defence for the Army and the Minister of National Defence for Air, but on the whole it has been an interesting and in some respects an informative statement. He spoke I think altogether for about eighty minutes.
The Canadian navy has grown greatly since the war commenced and it continues to grow.

The work of the minister and of his department has been greatly increased. Last year his estimates amounted to $258,542,713. This year they amount to $489,144,967.
In view of the development of . the navy, its activities in various theatres of war, and the large expenditures involved, I expected that the minister would have made a somewhat longer statement. He painted the picture in rather broad strokes. There are many details that remain to be filled in. Many members of the committee will probably ask for more detailed information about the activities of the navy and of its administration. There are many expenditures about which we should be furnished with more detailed particulars.
Last May, when the war appropriation bill was before the house in committee, several hon. members paid tribute to the officers and men of the Royal Canadian Navy. Those tributes were well deserved. I concur in them. There is nothing of merit that I can add to what was said on that occasion.
From time to time I read in the casualty lists the names of men of the Royal Canadian Navy who died serving their king and countiy. Some of these men came from the constituency which I have the honour to represent, which extends for over a hundred miles along the waters of the bay of Fundy. I realize there is little if anything I can say that will assuage the feelings of the wives and children, the mothers and fathers, the sisters and brothers of these gallant men. But I know they take some comfort from the fact that their loved ones died fighting for the freedom of mankind, the preservation of our Christian civilization, and the continued existence of Canada as a free nation within the British commonwealth of nations; and I know, too, that they take pride in the fact that their kinsfolk in this tragic but glorious struggle, did not shirk their duties but played the parts of men.
It must be the firm resolve of those of us who remain that the sacrifices they made have not been made in vain, but that this war be continued at all costs and all sacrifices until Hitler and all the evils which he and his nazi party stand for are banished from this earth.
I have no sympathy with the members of this house who say that Canada is doing too much for a country of her size. How can we do too much when we fight for our existence? How can we do too much when we consider the sacrifices that each of these men and the men in our army and our air force have made? We cannot limit with any financial yardstick our contribution to this cause when we consider the contributions of those men who, dying,

War Appropriation-Naval Services
have made us rarer gifts than gold. We cannot limit our monetary contribution in a cause in which they gave their lives.
There comes to my mind a statement which was made in this house about two years ago by the Right Hon. R. G. Menzies, then Prime Minister of Australia. He said, as reported in Hansard of 1941, at page 2632:
What does it matter if we come out into that world-
That is, the world after this war.
-bankrupt? What does it matter if we come out into that world with lower standards of material living than we have now? What does it matter if in that world the rich are not so rich? What does it matter if in the last resort the business of statesmanship in that new world becomes the business of sharing justly a new and honourable poverty? These things do not matter.
No; these things do not matter. We must keep faith with those who died in the defence of our country. We must be firmly resolved that the sacrifices they made were not and have not been made in vain.
On May 7 of last year, when the resolution to provide sums not exceeding $2,000,000,000 for the conduct of the war was before the house in committee-the amount asked for this year is $3,980,000,000 -the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services informed us, as reported in Hansard, at page 2239, that the total amount asked for naval services for the year ending March 31, 1943, was $258,542,713. On February 15, when the resolution for
the supplementary war appropriation for the past fiscal year was introduced, the Minister of Finance stated that he did not think there would be any difficulty about examining the expenditures of the then fiscal year when the main appropriation bill was before the house, because that was the time, he said, when the minister gave an account of his activities over the last year. It was incidental to the passing of the new estimates, he said, that the various ministers concerned should state what had been spent and what had been done.
Now that the estimates of the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services are before the house in committee, I would ask him to tell us what has been spent and what has been done by his department during the past fiscal year. In the first place I would ask him to furnish us with more detailed particulars of the manner in which the amounts listed under the eleven headings I have quoted above were spent; and in the second place I would ask him to tell us what the increases or decreases in his estimates for the coming year are due to. I presume, in some cases if not in all, there will be increases, since the estimated expenditures for the coming year are $489,144,967, or over twice as -much as last year's estimated expenditures.
The first heading in the list he furnished us with last year was civil salaries and wages, $3,768,000. This year, in the statement he furnished us with this evening, before he spoke, the amount is $3,645,222.28. I presume that must be approximately the correct amount, and the estimated expenditure for the present fiscal year he gives as $6,192,054, or an increase of $2,546,831.72.
With reference to last year's expenditure, will the minister tell us how many persons were employed and how much money was spent in salaries and wages at headquarters during the last fiscal year; how many persons were employed in each province and how much was spent in each province in
_ salaries and wages during the last fiscal year; how many persons were employed in the United States and how much was spent there in salaries and wages; how many were employed in Great Britain and how much was spent there in salaries and wages.

here and abroad, of the part Canada was playing in the war. According to a return tabled in this house on March 2 of this year, that board employed at that time about 121 persons and it had cost the country about $580,000 in a little less than six months. The supporters of the government in the house last month refused to permit the public accounts committee to investigate that expenditure. In addition to the information handed out by the war information board, each department of the government has its own publicity or propaganda department, or at any rate many of them have. Why it is necessary to have all these publicity departments or directorates of public information, and the war information bureau in addition, in view of the fact that the press has always been capable of obtaining news of the war and keeping the public informed on what is going on, is difficult for me to understand. Perhaps the minister will be able to explain it to this committee.
I would ask the minister to give the number of civilian personnel and the number of naval personnel employed in his publicity department, or in his directorate of public relations, during the past fiscal year or up to any subsequent date, and to let us know how the personnel is distributed by provinces or districts, how many are employed in Great Britain, and how many are employed in the United States.
Will the minister also furnish the committee with' the names and salaries of the civilian personnel and the naval personnel employed in this branch of his department; and in addition will he give us the travelling expenses and all other expenses and costs incurred by the civilian and naval personnel in this branch of his department during the past fiscal year, in addition to their salaries and wages?
The second heading of last year's estimated expenditures is pay and allowances, $53,195,000. In the statement we are furnished with this evening that amount is greatly increased. It is $63,256,432.19. There was a considerable increase in the amount expended over the amount that it was estimated would be expended, and the amount which it is estimated will be spent this year is $89,565,119, or a further increase of 826,328,686.81.
